subtopics.title: The Web: HTTP & HTTPS
subtopics.subtitle: Web architecture, HTTP messages, methods, status codes, connections, versions and HTTPS

concepts.text: Web Architecture

The World Wide Web is a distributed client-server application. A client (the browser) requests web pages from a web server; each page is a base HTML file that references further objects such as images, scripts and style sheets, each fetched separately. Every object is named by a Uniform Resource Locator (URL). HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer protocol that carries these requests and responses, normally over TCP port 80. HTTP is stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests from the same client.
Parts of a URL such as https://www.example.com:8443/docs/index.html?id=5#top:
items: Scheme (protocol): https, http, ftp; tells the browser which protocol and default port to use.
Host: www.example.com, resolved to an IP address through DNS.
Port: optional; defaults to 80 for http and 443 for https.
Path: /docs/index.html, the object on the server.
Query string: ?id=5, name-value parameters passed to the server; fragment #top is used only by the browser.

concepts.text: HTTP Request and Response Messages

HTTP/1.x messages are human-readable ASCII text. A request consists of a request line (method, URL, version, e.g. GET /index.html HTTP/1.1), header lines, a blank line (CRLF) and an optional body. A response consists of a status line (version, status code, phrase, e.g. HTTP/1.1 200 OK), header lines, a blank line and the body that carries the requested object.

rows: Retrieve a resource; parameters travel in the URL
Submit data (form, upload) in the body; creates or processes
Upload or replace the resource at the given URL
Remove the resource at the given URL
Same as GET but returns headers only, no body
Ask which methods and features the server supports
Apply a partial modification to a resource

concepts.text: Status codes are grouped into five classes by their first digit:
items: 1xx Informational: request received, continuing (100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols).
2xx Success: the request was received, understood and accepted.
3xx Redirection: further action (usually a new URL) is needed.
4xx Client error: the request is malformed or not permitted.
5xx Server error: a valid request that the server failed to fulfil.

rows: Request succeeded; object is in the body
Object has a new permanent URL (Location header)
Reply to a conditional GET; cached copy is still valid
Server could not parse the request
Authenticated or not, access is refused
Requested object does not exist on the server
Generic failure inside the server application
Server overloaded or down for maintenance

concepts.text: Common header lines:
items: Request: Host (mandatory in HTTP/1.1), User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Cookie, If-Modified-Since, Connection: keep-alive or close.
Response: Content-Type, Content-Length, Date, Server, Last-Modified, Set-Cookie, Location, Cache-Control, Expires.

concepts.text: Persistent vs Non-persistent Connections

With non-persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.0 default) a new TCP connection is opened for every object: one RTT for the TCP handshake and one RTT for the request and first bytes of the response, plus the transmission time of the object. Persistent HTTP (HTTP/1.1 default) keeps the connection open so later objects need only one RTT each; with pipelining the client sends all requests back to back and all referenced objects can arrive in about one RTT.

concepts.plainText: Non-persistent: T = (N + 1) x 2 RTT + transmission times, for a base file plus N objects

concepts.text: State, caching and proxies:
items: Cookies add state to stateless HTTP: the server sends Set-Cookie with an ID, the browser stores it and returns it in a Cookie header; the server keys a session (login, cart) on that ID in its back-end database.
Web cache (proxy server): sits between clients and origin servers, answers from its own store when it can, cutting response time and access-link traffic.
Conditional GET: the cache sends If-Modified-Since; the server answers 304 Not Modified (no body) if the object is unchanged, otherwise 200 with the new object.
Forward proxies serve an organisation's clients; reverse proxies sit in front of servers for load balancing, TLS termination and caching.

rows: No (one request at a time; pipelining rarely used)
Removed at HTTP level, remains in TCP

concepts.text: HTTPS is HTTP carried over TLS (formerly SSL), on TCP port 443; in outline:
items: TCP handshake, then TLS handshake: client hello (supported ciphers), server hello plus the server's X.509 certificate.
The browser verifies the certificate: signed by a trusted certificate authority, not expired or revoked, and the name matches the requested host.
Key exchange (e.g. ECDHE) establishes a shared session key; all HTTP data is then encrypted and integrity-protected with symmetric ciphers such as AES-GCM.
HTTPS provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication; it does not hide the server's IP address.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: HTTP and HTTPS
Your notes on HTTP and HTTPS, cleaned up and corrected:
items: HTTP uses TCP port 80 and HTTPS uses TCP port 443 by default; a port written in the URL overrides the default, as in http://intranet.local:8080/.
HTTP is stateless: every request is handled on its own and the server remembers nothing between requests unless the application adds cookies or tokens.

HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 are text-based, so a packet analyser such as Wireshark shows requests, cookies and typed passwords in plain view. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use binary frames and in practice always run over TLS.
PUT does not update part of a resource: it replaces the whole resource at that URL, or creates it. Partial changes use PATCH, and POST submits data (such as a form) for the server to process.
HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. The SSL versions are obsolete and prohibited (SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are broken), so an 'SSL certificate' today is really a certificate used with TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.
Use HTTPS for every page, not only for passwords and card numbers: browsers mark plain-HTTP pages 'Not secure', and without TLS anyone on the path can read or silently change any page.

concepts.text:
C: GET /news/today.html HTTP/1.1
C: Host: www.example.com
C: User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
C: Accept: text/html
C: (blank line ends the headers; a GET has no body)
S: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
S: Date: Sun, 27 Sep 2026 09:00:00 GMT
S: Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
S: Content-Length: 5120
S: Cache-Control: max-age=600
S: (blank line, then exactly 5120 bytes of HTML)

A method is safe if it only reads, so the server's state does not change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. A method is idempotent if sending the same request several times leaves the server in the same state as sending it once: all the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE. POST is neither, so submitting an order form twice can create two orders. That is why a browser or proxy may retry an idempotent request after a dropped connection on its own, while a browser asks before re-sending a POST, and why a plain link (a GET) must never perform an action such as deleting a record.

rows: A POST or PUT created a new resource; Location gives its URL
Success with no body, for example after a DELETE
Reply to a Range request, used to resume a download
Like 302 / 301, but the method and body must be kept
The resource exists but does not accept this method
The client has exceeded a rate limit
A proxy got an invalid reply / no reply in time from the upstream server

concepts.plainText: T = 2 RTT + ceiling(N / M) x 2 RTT for a base file plus N small objects fetched over M parallel non-persistent connections

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: base page + 10 small objects on one server
RTT = 20 ms, DNS lookup = 50 ms, plain HTTP (no TLS), transmission times negligible
Non-persistent, serial:      50 + 2x20 + 10 x 2x20        = 490 ms
Non-persistent, 5 parallel:  50 + 2x20 + ceil(10/5) x 2x20 = 170 ms
Persistent, no pipelining:   50 + 2x20 + 10 x 20          = 290 ms
Persistent, pipelined:       50 + 2x20 + 1 x 20           = 110 ms
The 2x20 term is the base file: 1 RTT for TCP setup + 1 RTT for request/response

Worked example 2: an institutional web cache
Requests 30/s, average object 0.5 Mbit, access link 20 Mbps
Access-link load without cache = 30 x 0.5 / 20 = 0.75 (75 %)
Cache hit ratio h = 0.6, so only the 40 % misses cross the link
Access-link load with cache = (1 - 0.6) x 0.75 = 0.30 (30 %)
Hit served over the LAN in 10 ms; miss via the origin in 400 ms
Average response = 0.6 x 10 + 0.4 x 400 = 6 + 160 = 166 ms

concepts.plainText: Average response time = h x hit time + (1 - h) x miss time, where h is the cache hit ratio

concepts.text: Headers that make virtual hosting, caching and cookies work:
items: Host: www.example.com lets one IP address serve many websites (virtual hosting); HTTP/1.1 requires it in every request.
Cache-Control: max-age=600 lets a cache reuse its copy for 600 s; no-cache allows storing but forces revalidation before each reuse; no-store forbids storing at all.
ETag and If-None-Match: the server labels a version, for example ETag: "v7"; a cache revalidates with If-None-Match: "v7" and receives 304 Not Modified if its copy is still current.

Set-Cookie attributes: Expires or Max-Age (without either it is a session cookie, deleted when the browser session ends), Secure (send only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (hidden from page scripts), SameSite (limits sending on cross-site requests), Domain and Path.
Transfer-Encoding: chunked sends a body of unknown length as size-prefixed pieces ending with a zero-length chunk, so the persistent connection can carry the next response.

concepts.text: Versions, set-up cost and certificates (round trips until the first byte of a small page, transmission ignored):
items: HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP with TLS 1.3: 1 RTT for TCP + 1 RTT for TLS + 1 RTT for the request = 3 RTT. TLS 1.2 needs a 2-RTT handshake, giving 4 RTT.
HTTP/3 over QUIC merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into 1 RTT, so the first byte arrives after 2 RTT; with 0-RTT resumption the request travels in the very first flight.

HTTP/2 multiplexes streams as binary frames over one TCP connection, but one lost TCP segment stalls every stream until it is retransmitted; QUIC recovers losses per stream, so only the affected stream waits.

HTTP/1.1 pipelining sends several requests without waiting, but responses must return in request order, so one slow response blocks the rest; browsers disabled it and opened about six parallel connections per host instead.

Certificate check: the chain must lead to a trusted root CA, the certificate must be in date and not revoked, and its Subject Alternative Name must match the host. The Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header then tells the browser to use only HTTPS for that site.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: counting N objects instead of N + 1 (the base file is also fetched); charging a new TCP handshake to every object on a persistent connection; and believing HTTPS hides everything. An observer still sees the server's IP address and usually the host name (in the DNS query and the TLS SNI field), but not the path, query string, headers, cookies or body.

formulas.plainText: Non-persistent, serial, transmission ignored: T = (N + 1) x 2 RTT
Persistent without pipelining: T = 2 RTT + N x RTT
Persistent with pipelining: T is about 3 RTT for base file plus all objects

notes.text: Remember the non-persistent cost as 2 RTT per object (one for TCP setup, one for request/response). MCQs often give a page with a base file and several images and ask for the total time.
401 Unauthorized means authentication is missing or wrong; 403 Forbidden means the server refuses even though it understood who you are. Do not swap them.
HTTP itself is stateless; cookies, sessions and tokens are add-ons that let applications remember users across requests.

formulas.title: Non-persistent HTTP time
formulas.description: Total time to fetch a base file and N referenced objects when each object uses a new TCP connection serially.

formulas.title: Persistent HTTP time
formulas.description: With a persistent connection and no pipelining, only the first object pays the TCP handshake RTT.

formulas.title: Pipelined HTTP time
formulas.description: With persistence and pipelining, all referenced objects are requested together and arrive in roughly one extra RTT.

flashcards.front: What does HTTP status code 304 mean?
flashcards.back: Not Modified: the reply to a conditional GET telling the cache its stored copy is still valid, so no body is sent.

flashcards.front: How does a website remember a logged-in user when HTTP is stateless?
flashcards.back: With cookies: the server sends Set-Cookie with a session ID and the browser returns it in a Cookie header on every later request.

flashcards.front: Which transport does HTTP/3 use?
flashcards.back: QUIC running over UDP, with TLS 1.3 built in and independent streams that avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.

flashcards.front: Difference between GET and POST?
flashcards.back: GET retrieves a resource with parameters in the URL and is safe and idempotent; POST sends data in the request body to be processed and is not idempotent.

questions.questionText: A web page consists of a base HTML file and 5 referenced images. The RTT is 20 ms and transmission times are negligible. Using non-persistent HTTP with serial connections, how long does it take to fetch the whole page?
options: 120 ms
240 ms
140 ms
60 ms
questions.explanation: Each of the 6 objects needs 2 RTT (TCP setup plus request/response): 6 x 2 x 20 ms = 240 ms. Persistent pipelined HTTP would need only about 3 RTT = 60 ms.

questions.questionText: A proxy cache sends a conditional GET with an If-Modified-Since header, and the object has not changed on the origin server. Which status code does the server return?
options: 200 OK
301 Moved Permanently
404 Not Found
304 Not Modified
questions.explanation: 304 Not Modified tells the cache its copy is still valid and carries no body, saving bandwidth.

questions.questionText: Which application-layer protocol transfers web pages from a web server to a browser?
options: FTP
HTTP
DNS
SMTP
questions.explanation: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) carries the browser's requests and the server's responses for web pages and their objects, by default on TCP port 80. FTP transfers files, DNS resolves names and SMTP sends mail.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
options: HTTPS is a faster version of HTTP that compresses every page
HTTP uses port 443 while HTTPS uses port 80
HTTPS carries HTTP inside a TLS connection, so the traffic is encrypted and the server proves its identity with a certificate
HTTPS encrypts only the password fields of a form
questions.explanation: HTTPS is ordinary HTTP sent through TLS (the successor of SSL) on port 443: TLS encrypts and integrity-protects the whole exchange and authenticates the server with its X.509 certificate. Plain HTTP uses port 80 and sends everything in clear text.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes how HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) protects the data it carries?
options: Public-key cryptography and the server's certificate are used in the handshake to agree on session keys, and the page data is then encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher
Every HTTP message is encrypted with the server's RSA public key, and no symmetric cipher is used
The browser and the server share one fixed symmetric key that is built into the browser for each website
Only the URL is encrypted; the headers and the body travel in plain text
questions.explanation: TLS is a hybrid scheme: asymmetric cryptography (certificate verification plus an ECDHE key exchange) sets up fresh session keys, and the bulk data is protected with a symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM, which is far faster. The whole HTTP message, including the path, headers and body, is encrypted.

questions.questionText: For the URL http://www.example.com/docs/page.html?lang=en#section2, which part is used only by the browser and is never sent to the server in the HTTP request?
options: ?lang=en, the query string
/docs/page.html, the path
www.example.com, the host name
#section2, the fragment
questions.explanation: The browser sends the path and query in the request line (GET /docs/page.html?lang=en HTTP/1.1) and the host name in the Host header. The fragment only tells the browser which part of the page to show, so it never leaves the browser.

questions.questionText: A user opens the URL http://intranet.local:8080/reports. To which TCP port on the server does the browser connect?
questions.explanation: A port written after the host name in the URL overrides the scheme's default. Without it, http would use port 80 and https port 443.

questions.questionText: Which line is a correctly formed HTTP/1.1 request line?
options: GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
HTTP/1.1 GET /index.html
GET HTTP/1.1 www.example.com/index.html
questions.explanation: A request line is the method, the request target and the version separated by spaces, for example GET /index.html HTTP/1.1; the host goes in the separate Host header. HTTP/1.1 200 OK is a response status line.

questions.questionText: Which HTTP method asks for the same status line and headers that a GET would return, but without the message body?
options: OPTIONS
TRACE
HEAD
PATCH
questions.explanation: HEAD lets a client check whether a resource exists, its size (Content-Length) or its Last-Modified date without downloading it. OPTIONS lists the supported methods, TRACE echoes the request back and PATCH partially modifies a resource.

questions.questionText: Which HTTP method is idempotent but NOT safe?
options: GET
HEAD
POST
DELETE
questions.explanation: DELETE changes server state, so it is not safe, but deleting the same resource twice leaves the same state as deleting it once, so it is idempotent (PUT is the other such method). GET and HEAD are both safe and idempotent, and POST is neither.

questions.questionText: Which of these status codes reports a failure on the server side rather than a problem with the client's request?
options: 400 Bad Request
502 Bad Gateway
404 Not Found
429 Too Many Requests
questions.explanation: 5xx codes are server errors; 502 means a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from the upstream server. Every 4xx code, including 400, 404 and 429, reports a problem with the client's request.

questions.questionText: A reverse proxy forwards a request to an application server, which does not reply before the proxy's time limit expires. Which status code does the proxy return to the browser?
options: 408 Request Timeout
502 Bad Gateway
504 Gateway Timeout
503 Service Unavailable
questions.explanation: 504 means a gateway or proxy did not receive a timely response from the upstream server. 408 is used when the client is too slow to send its request, 502 when the upstream reply is invalid, and 503 when the server itself is overloaded or in maintenance.

questions.questionText:
A browser requests http://old.example.com/about and receives this response:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://www.example.com/about
What does the browser do next?
options: It sends a new request to https://www.example.com/about and may remember the redirect for later visits
It displays the body of the 301 response as the page
It keeps retrying http://old.example.com/about until it gets 200 OK
It treats the page as deleted and shows an error
questions.explanation: A 3xx code means further action is needed, and the browser follows the Location header automatically. Because 301 is permanent, browsers and search engines may cache it and update their links, unlike a temporary 302 or 307.

questions.questionText: Why must every HTTP/1.1 request carry a Host header?
options: So that the server learns the client's IP address and can send the reply
So that a proxy knows which TCP port to open to the origin server
So that the server knows which browser and version sent the request
So that one server at a single IP address can host many websites and know which site each request is for
questions.explanation: Many sites often share one IP address (virtual hosting) and the request line carries only the path, so the Host header names the wanted site. The client's address comes from the IP header and the browser type from User-Agent.

questions.questionText: A server builds a large page on the fly and does not know its length when it starts sending on a persistent HTTP/1.1 connection. How can the client tell where the body ends while the connection stays open?
options: The body ends at the first blank line after the headers
The server uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked, sending each piece with its size and ending with a zero-length chunk
The client stops reading when no data has arrived for one RTT
The server sends a 100 Continue status line after the last byte
questions.explanation: Chunked transfer coding frames the body as size-prefixed chunks followed by a final chunk of size 0, so the end of the message is explicit and the connection can carry the next response. The blank line marks the end of the headers, not of the body.

questions.questionText: Which Set-Cookie attribute stops scripts running in the page from reading the cookie, limiting the damage of a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack?
options: Secure
SameSite=Strict
HttpOnly
Max-Age
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so injected JavaScript cannot steal a session ID. Secure only restricts sending to HTTPS, SameSite limits sending on cross-site requests and Max-Age sets the lifetime.

questions.questionText: A server sends Set-Cookie: sid=81fa2 with no Expires or Max-Age attribute. What kind of cookie is this?
options: A session cookie, deleted when the browser session ends
A permanent cookie that never expires
A cookie that expires after exactly 24 hours
An invalid cookie that the browser discards
questions.explanation: Without Expires or Max-Age the browser keeps the cookie only for the current browsing session. Adding either attribute makes it a persistent cookie kept until that date or age.

questions.questionText: A web page has a base HTML file and 7 small referenced objects, all on the same server. RTT = 25 ms and transmission times are negligible. Using plain HTTP (no TLS) with a persistent connection that must first be opened, and no pipelining (one request at a time), how long does it take to fetch the whole page, counting the TCP handshake but no DNS lookup?
options: 400 ms
200 ms
75 ms
225 ms
questions.explanation: One RTT sets up TCP, then each of the 8 objects costs one request/response RTT: T = 2 RTT + 7 RTT = 9 x 25 ms = 225 ms. Non-persistent HTTP would take 8 x 2 x 25 = 400 ms, and pipelining would cut it to about 3 RTT = 75 ms.

questions.questionText: A browser with an empty DNS cache follows a link to a page made of a base HTML file and 12 small images on the same server. The DNS lookup takes 40 ms in total, the RTT to the web server is 30 ms and transmission times are negligible. The browser uses non-persistent plain HTTP (no TLS) with up to 4 parallel TCP connections, and each connection needs a TCP handshake. How long does it take until the whole page has arrived?
options: 240 ms
820 ms
280 ms
190 ms
questions.explanation: T = DNS + 2 RTT for the base file + ceil(12 / 4) x 2 RTT = 40 + 60 + 3 x 60 = 280 ms. Serial non-persistent HTTP would need 40 + 13 x 60 = 820 ms, and forgetting the DNS lookup gives 240 ms.

questions.questionText: A page has a 50 kB base HTML file and 4 images of 100 kB each on the same server. RTT = 50 ms and the link rate is 8 Mbps (1 kB = 1000 bytes, 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s); request sizes, headers and processing are negligible, there is no DNS lookup or TLS, and one TCP handshake (1 RTT) opens the connection. A response starts arriving one RTT after its request is sent, or right after the previous response if the link is still busy, so pipelined responses follow one another back to back. With persistent HTTP and pipelining (all image requests sent together once the base file has arrived), how long does the whole page take?
options: 600 ms
750 ms
950 ms
150 ms
questions.explanation: Transmission: base 50,000 x 8 / (8 x 10^6) = 50 ms and each image 100 ms. T = 1 RTT (TCP) + (1 RTT + 50 ms) for the base + (1 RTT + 4 x 100 ms) for the pipelined images = 50 + 100 + 450 = 600 ms; without pipelining it is 50 + 100 + 4 x 150 = 750 ms.

questions.questionText: RTT = 40 ms and transmission times are negligible. A browser fetches one small page over a brand-new connection (i) with HTTP/2 over TCP and a full TLS 1.3 handshake, and (ii) with HTTP/3 over QUIC without 0-RTT resumption. Measured from the first packet the client sends (the server address is already known, so no DNS lookup), when does the first byte of the page arrive in each case?
options: (i) 160 ms, (ii) 80 ms
(i) 120 ms, (ii) 80 ms
(i) 120 ms, (ii) 40 ms
(i) 80 ms, (ii) 40 ms
questions.explanation: (i) 1 RTT TCP + 1 RTT TLS 1.3 + 1 RTT request = 3 x 40 = 120 ms; (ii) QUIC merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into 1 RTT, plus 1 RTT for the request = 80 ms. 160 ms would need TLS 1.2's 2-RTT handshake, and 40 ms needs 0-RTT resumption.

questions.questionText: An HTTP/2 connection is carrying 10 streams when a single TCP segment belonging to one of them is lost. What happens, and how does HTTP/3 behave differently?
options: Only the affected stream stalls in HTTP/2 as well, because every HTTP/2 frame carries a stream ID
HTTP/2 resends all 10 streams from the beginning, while HTTP/3 opens a new connection for each stream
Nothing stalls in either version, because both use forward error correction instead of retransmission
All 10 streams stall until the segment is retransmitted, because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order; QUIC recovers losses per stream, so only the affected stream waits
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer, but all its streams share one TCP byte stream, so a missing segment holds back the data of every stream in the receive buffer. QUIC runs over UDP and orders data per stream, so a loss delays only the stream it belongs to.

questions.questionText: Which feature was introduced by HTTP/2 and was NOT available in HTTP/1.1?
options: Multiplexing many concurrent requests and responses as interleaved binary frames over one TCP connection
Persistent connections that carry several requests and responses
The mandatory Host header that allows virtual hosting
Running over UDP by means of the QUIC protocol
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames tagged with stream IDs, interleaves them on one connection and compresses headers with HPACK. Persistent connections and the Host header already existed in HTTP/1.1, and QUIC over UDP belongs to HTTP/3.

questions.questionText: HTTP/1.1 allows pipelining, yet browsers turned it off. What was the main limitation that made it of little use?
options: Each pipelined request needs its own new TCP connection
Only POST requests may be pipelined, while most page objects are fetched with GET
Responses must return in the order of the requests, so one slow response holds up every response queued behind it
Pipelining works only when the server closes the connection after each response
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 responses carry no request identifier, so they must come back in order; a slow first object causes head-of-line blocking, and faulty proxies made things worse. Browsers opened several parallel connections instead, and HTTP/2 solved the problem with multiplexed streams.

questions.questionText: An institution's users make 40 web requests per second for objects of 400 kbit on average, over a 20 Mbps access link. A web cache with a hit ratio of 0.45 is installed. Assuming 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s and that only cache misses cross the access link, what is the access-link utilisation with the cache?
questions.explanation: Without the cache the load is 40 x 0.4 Mbit / 20 Mbps = 0.8. Only the misses (1 - 0.45 = 0.55) use the link: 0.55 x 0.8 = 0.44, i.e. 44%.

questions.questionText: A proxy cache has a hit ratio of 0.7. A hit is served in 5 ms, while a miss, which must go to the origin server, takes 250 ms. What is the average response time seen by the users?
options: 250 ms
questions.explanation: T_avg = h x T_hit + (1 - h) x T_miss = 0.7 x 5 + 0.3 x 250 = 3.5 + 75 = 78.5 ms. Swapping h and 1 - h gives 176.5 ms, and a plain average of the two times gives 127.5 ms.

questions.questionText: A cache holds a copy of an object that the server labelled with ETag: "v7". Which request header does the cache send to ask the server whether that copy is still current?
options: If-None-Match: "v7"
If-Modified-Since: "v7"
ETag: "v7"
Cache-Control: no-store
questions.explanation: If-None-Match carries the stored entity tag; the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body if the tag still matches, or 200 with the new version. If-Modified-Since takes a date rather than a tag, and ETag itself is a response header.

questions.questionText: An online bank wants to make sure that no browser or proxy cache ever stores its account-statement pages. Which Cache-Control directive should these responses carry?
options: no-cache
no-store
max-age=0
public
questions.explanation: no-store forbids every cache from keeping the response. no-cache and max-age=0 still allow the copy to be stored and only require revalidation before reuse, and public explicitly allows shared caches to store it.

questions.questionText: Where is a reverse proxy placed, and what is it typically used for?
options: Inside each user's browser, to store cookies for later visits
At the edge of the client organisation, forwarding its users' requests to any website on the Internet
In front of one or more web servers, receiving client requests on their behalf for load balancing, caching and TLS termination
Inside the DNS hierarchy, translating host names into server IP addresses
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy represents the servers: clients connect to it as if it were the site, and it spreads requests over back-end servers, caches responses and handles HTTPS. A proxy at the client organisation's edge that serves its own users is a forward proxy.

questions.questionText: During an HTTPS connection to https://bank.example.com, which check does the browser perform on the server's certificate?
options: That it contains the server's private key
That it was issued within the last 24 hours
That it is signed with the browser's own private key
That it chains to a trusted root CA, is within its validity period, is not revoked and names bank.example.com as a subject
questions.explanation: The browser checks the signature chain up to a root CA in its trust store, the validity dates, the revocation status and that the Subject Alternative Name matches the host. A certificate carries only the public key; the private key never leaves the server.

questions.questionText: A user on public Wi-Fi opens https://bank.example.com/accounts?id=123. Assuming ordinary unencrypted DNS and no Encrypted Client Hello, what can a passive eavesdropper on the Wi-Fi still learn?
options: The server's IP address and the host name bank.example.com, but not the path, query string, headers or cookies
The full URL including ?id=123, because TLS never encrypts URLs
Nothing at all, not even the server's IP address
The cookies, because TLS encrypts only the message body
questions.explanation: IP headers must stay readable for routing, and the host name leaks through the DNS query and the TLS SNI field. Everything inside the HTTP message, including the request line with the path and query, the headers and the cookies, is encrypted by TLS.

questions.questionText: Which statement about HTTP is NOT correct?
options: HTTP is stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests from a client
The request line and headers of HTTP/1.1 messages are human-readable ASCII text
HTTP/1.1 closes the TCP connection after every response unless the client asks otherwise
Without TLS, the contents of HTTP messages can be read by anyone on the path
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default, and either side sends Connection: close to end one. The other three statements are true; statelessness is the reason cookies are needed.

subtopics.title: File Transfer & Remote Access: FTP, PuTTY & WinSCP
subtopics.subtitle: FTP modes and ports, TFTP, SFTP vs FTPS, Telnet vs SSH, PuTTY, WinSCP and SCP

concepts.text: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)

FTP transfers files between a client and a server over TCP using two separate connections, so its control information is sent out-of-band. The control connection (server port 21) stays open for the whole session and carries commands and replies; a data connection (port 20 in active mode) is opened for each file or directory listing and closed afterwards. FTP is stateful: the server tracks the current directory and the authenticated user. Username, password and data all travel in plaintext.

rows: Client sends PORT with its IP and port
Client sends PASV; server replies with IP and port
Server, from port 20 to the client
Client, to a high port on the server
Often blocked, since the connection comes inward to the client
Friendly to clients behind firewalls and NAT
Default in browsers and most modern clients

concepts.text: Transfer types and common commands:
items: ASCII (TYPE A) mode converts line endings between systems and suits text files; binary / image (TYPE I) mode copies bytes unchanged and must be used for executables, images and archives.
Protocol commands: USER, PASS, LIST, RETR (download), STOR (upload), CWD, PWD, DELE, MKD, TYPE, PORT, PASV, QUIT.
Typical command-line client commands: open, get, put, mget, mput, ls, cd, binary, ascii, bye.
Reply codes are three-digit, e.g. 220 service ready, 230 user logged in, 331 password required, 226 transfer complete, 530 not logged in.

concepts.text: TFTP (Trivial FTP) is a minimal file-transfer protocol that runs over UDP port 69. It has no authentication and no directory listing; it sends 512-byte blocks using stop-and-wait acknowledgements. It is used for booting diskless hosts (PXE) and for loading configuration or firmware onto routers and switches.
Secure File Transfer

rows: Subsystem of SSH (not FTP at all)
21 explicit (AUTH TLS) or 990 implicit, plus data ports
One channel for commands and data

concepts.text: SCP (Secure Copy) also runs over SSH on port 22 and copies files with a simple syntax such as scp report.pdf user@server:/home/user/. It is fast and scriptable but offers no directory browsing, resume or remote file management, which is why SFTP has largely replaced it.
Remote Login: Telnet vs SSH
How SSH secures a session:
items: Transport layer: server authentication with a host key (the client checks the key fingerprint on first connect), key exchange and encryption.
User authentication layer: password, or public-key authentication in which the server holds the user's public key and the client proves possession of the private key.
Connection layer: multiplexes channels for shell sessions, file transfer and port forwarding over one encrypted connection.

concepts.text: PuTTY and WinSCP
PuTTY is a free Windows terminal client for remote login:
items: Supports SSH, Telnet, rlogin, raw TCP and serial connections (useful for router console cables).
Saved sessions store host name, port, protocol and settings for one-click reconnection.
PuTTYgen generates RSA, ECDSA or Ed25519 key pairs and saves private keys in .ppk format; Pageant is the SSH agent that holds keys in memory.
Port forwarding: local, remote and dynamic (SOCKS) tunnels through the SSH connection; companion tools pscp and psftp do command-line file transfer.

concepts.text: WinSCP is a free graphical file-transfer client for Windows:
items: Supports SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and Amazon S3.
Two-panel (Commander) or Explorer-style interface with drag-and-drop between local and remote folders.
Directory synchronisation (local to remote, remote to local, or both), built-in text editor and scripting for automation.
Can import PuTTY sessions and use .ppk keys, and can open a PuTTY terminal on the same server.

concepts.plainText: TCP connections for n files in one FTP session = 1 control + n data

concepts.text: Going Deeper: FTP, SSH, PuTTY and WinSCP
Your notes on file transfer and remote access, cleaned up and corrected:
items: FTP uses TCP port 21 for its control connection (commands and replies) and a separate data connection for each file or listing. Port 20 is the server's data port only in active mode; in passive mode the data connection goes to a high port chosen by the server.
FTP normally needs a user name and password, but public servers may allow anonymous FTP (user name 'anonymous'). Either way the whole session, password included, crosses the network in plain text.
Active FTP: the server opens the data connection back to the client. Passive FTP: the client opens both connections, which is why passive mode works through NAT and client-side firewalls.
SFTP and SCP run inside SSH on TCP port 22, so both the login and the file data are encrypted; they, and SSH itself, have replaced FTP and Telnet for administration work.
PuTTY is a terminal client for remote command-line sessions (SSH, Telnet, serial); WinSCP is a graphical file-transfer client (SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS). Both use PuTTY's .ppk private-key format.

concepts.text:
S: 220 ftp.example.com FTP server ready
C: USER alice                 S: 331 Password required
C: PASS ********              S: 230 User logged in
C: TYPE I                     S: 200 Type set to I (binary)
C: PASV                       S: 227 Entering Passive Mode (203,0,113,8,197,143)
   client computes 197 x 256 + 143 = 50575 and connects to 203.0.113.8:50575
C: RETR report.pdf            S: 150 Opening BINARY mode data connection
   the file flows over the data connection, which then closes
                              S: 226 Transfer complete
C: QUIT                       S: 221 Goodbye

rows: Positive preliminary: action started, another reply will follow
Positive completion: the action is done
200 OK, 220 ready, 226 transfer complete, 227 passive mode, 230 logged in
Positive intermediate: send the next command
Transient negative: may succeed if retried later
421 service not available, 425 cannot open data connection, 426 transfer aborted
Permanent negative: do not repeat unchanged
500 syntax error, 530 not logged in, 550 file unavailable

concepts.plainText: Data port p = 256 x p1 + p2, where p1 and p2 are the last two numbers of a PORT command or a 227 PASV reply

concepts.text: TFTP (RFC 1350) has only five message types: read request (RRQ), write request (WRQ), DATA, ACK and ERROR. The client sends its request to UDP port 69, and the server answers from a new ephemeral port that is used for the rest of the transfer. Data moves in numbered 512-byte blocks with stop-and-wait: each block is acknowledged before the next is sent, and is retransmitted if the ACK does not arrive in time. A block shorter than 512 bytes ends the transfer, so a file whose size is an exact multiple of 512 needs a final zero-length block.

concepts.plainText: TFTP DATA blocks B = floor(F / 512) + 1 for an F-byte file; stop-and-wait transfer time T is about B x RTT

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: active mode, client sends PORT 172,16,4,20,39,16
Client address = 172.16.4.20; port = 39 x 256 + 16 = 9984 + 16 = 10000
Server opens the data connection from its port 20 to 172.16.4.20:10000
Worked example 2: TFTP, 1800-byte file, RTT = 10 ms, 512-byte blocks
Blocks = floor(1800 / 512) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4 (512, 512, 512 and 264 bytes)
Time = 4 x 10 ms = 40 ms; throughput = 1800 x 8 / 0.040 s = 360 kbit/s
Worked example 3: one FTP session with 1 listing and 4 downloads
TCP connections = 1 control + (1 + 4) data = 6

rows: SSH, Telnet, rlogin, raw TCP and serial sessions
Creates key pairs; imports OpenSSH keys and saves them as .ppk
Holds decrypted private keys for PuTTY, WinSCP and Plink
SCP / SFTP copies from scripts and batch files
SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV, S3; synchronisation and scripting

concepts.text: SSH features you use through PuTTY and WinSCP:
items: Host-key check: on first contact the client shows the server's key fingerprint; once accepted, the key is cached, and a changed key triggers a warning that may mean a man-in-the-middle.

Public-key login: the server keeps the user's public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the private key stays on the client (in .ppk format for PuTTY), and the client proves it holds the key by signing a challenge.

Local port forwarding (PuTTY: Connection > SSH > Tunnels, or ssh -L 8080:10.0.0.5:80 gateway): connections to a local port are carried through the encrypted session, and the SSH server opens the onward connection.
scp syntax: scp [-P port] [-r] source destination, where a remote side is written user@host:path and the first argument is always the source.
WinSCP extras: Commander and Explorer interfaces, directory synchronisation ('Keep remote directory up to date'), a built-in editor, and scripting with winscp.com /script=file.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: port 20 is not used in passive mode; FTPS (FTP plus TLS, on port 21 with AUTH TLS or implicitly on 990) is not SFTP (an SSH subsystem on port 22); PuTTY's host-key cache holds server keys, while authorized_keys holds users' public keys; and a private key is never copied to the server.

For PORT and PASV numbers, the first four values are the IP address and the port is 256 x fifth value + sixth value. For TFTP, divide the file size by 512, round down and add one to get the number of DATA blocks.

formulas.plainText: Connections = 1 control connection + n data connections
Transfer time = 8 x file size in bytes / rate in bit/s

notes.text: Port pairs to memorise: FTP 20 data and 21 control, TFTP UDP 69, SSH/SFTP/SCP 22, Telnet 23, FTPS implicit 990.
SFTP is not FTP over SSL. SFTP is an SSH subsystem on port 22; FTP over SSL/TLS is FTPS.
PuTTY is mainly a terminal (SSH/Telnet) client, while WinSCP is a graphical file-transfer client; both are Windows tools that speak SSH.

formulas.title: FTP connection count
formulas.description: One persistent control connection plus a fresh data connection for each of the n files or listings transferred.

formulas.title: File transfer time
formulas.description: Approximate time to move a file of F bytes over a path with throughput R bit/s, ignoring setup delays.

flashcards.front: In passive FTP, who opens the data connection?
flashcards.back: The client, after the PASV command, connects to a port the server announced; this works through client-side firewalls and NAT.

flashcards.front: What is PuTTYgen used for?
flashcards.back: Generating SSH public/private key pairs (saved as .ppk) for key-based login with PuTTY and WinSCP.

flashcards.front: Why should binary mode be used to transfer a ZIP file by FTP?
flashcards.back: ASCII mode rewrites line-ending bytes, which corrupts non-text files; binary mode copies every byte unchanged.

questions.questionText: An FTP client behind a NAT firewall cannot accept incoming connections. Which FTP mode lets it transfer files, and how?
options: Active mode; the server connects from port 20 to the client
Active mode; the client sends PORT and opens port 21
Passive mode; the client sends PASV and opens the data connection to the server
Passive mode; the server opens a UDP connection to port 69
questions.explanation: In passive mode the server announces a port in its PASV reply and the client opens the data connection outward, which NAT and firewalls allow.

questions.questionText: Which transport protocol and port does TFTP use?
options: UDP port 69
TCP port 21
TCP port 69
UDP port 20
questions.explanation: TFTP is a lightweight protocol over UDP port 69, with no authentication, used for network booting and device configuration.

questions.questionText: What does FTP stand for?
options: File Transmission Protocol
File Transfer Protocol
Fast Transfer Program
File Transfer Process
questions.explanation: FTP, the File Transfer Protocol (RFC 959), copies files between a client and a server over TCP, using port 21 for commands and a separate data connection for the files themselves.

questions.questionText: What is PuTTY mainly used for?
options: Logging in to a remote computer's command line over SSH (it also supports Telnet and serial connections)
Hosting and managing websites
Encrypting files stored on a local disk
Capturing and analysing network packets
questions.explanation: PuTTY is a free terminal client for Windows that opens remote shell sessions, mostly over SSH on port 22, and also Telnet, rlogin, raw TCP and serial lines. Packet capture is Wireshark's job.

questions.questionText: Which Windows tool gives a graphical, drag-and-drop interface for copying files to and from a server securely over SSH (SFTP or SCP)?
options: PuTTY
Cisco Packet Tracer
WinSCP
DNS Manager
questions.explanation: WinSCP is a graphical file-transfer client for SFTP and SCP (plus FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and S3). PuTTY is a terminal client for remote command-line sessions, Packet Tracer is a network simulator and DNS Manager administers DNS zones.

questions.questionText: Which statement about FTP's two connections is correct?
options: Commands and file data share a single TCP connection on port 21
One data connection stays open for the whole session, and a new control connection is opened for each command
Both connections use UDP so that files can move faster
The control connection to server port 21 stays open for the whole session, while each file transfer or directory listing uses its own data connection
questions.explanation: FTP sends its control information out of band: commands and replies travel on the long-lived control connection (port 21), and a separate data connection (from port 20 in active mode) is opened and closed for each file or listing.

questions.questionText: In active-mode FTP, which side opens the data connection?
options: The client, from a random port to the server's port 20
The server, from its port 20 to the IP address and port that the client gave in its PORT command
The client, to a high port that the server announced in its PASV reply
The server, by reusing the control connection on port 21
questions.explanation: In active mode the client listens on a port and announces it with PORT, and the server connects out from port 20. The client connecting to a port announced by the server is passive mode (PASV).

questions.questionText:
An FTP server answers the PASV command with:
227 Entering Passive Mode (192,168,10,5,195,80)
To which address and port does the client open the data connection?
questions.explanation: The six numbers are four address bytes and two port bytes: port = 195 x 256 + 80 = 49,920 + 80 = 50,000. Writing the two bytes side by side (19580) or adding them (275) are common slips, and port 20 belongs to active mode.

questions.questionText: An FTP client at 10.0.0.7 (no NAT) sends the command PORT 10,0,0,7,19,137 and then RETR report.pdf. Which TCP connection carries the file?
options: A connection opened by the server from its port 20 to 10.0.0.7 port 5001
A connection opened by the client from 10.0.0.7 port 5001 to the server's port 20
The existing control connection between the client and server port 21
A connection opened by the server from its port 20 to 10.0.0.7 port 19137
questions.explanation: PORT gives the client's listening address and port: 19 x 256 + 137 = 4864 + 137 = 5001. In active mode the server opens the data connection from port 20 to 10.0.0.7:5001 and sends the file over it.

questions.questionText: Which FTP protocol command uploads (stores) a file from the client to the server?
options: RETR
LIST
DELE
STOR
questions.explanation: STOR uploads a file and RETR downloads one; a command-line client's put and get are translated into STOR and RETR. LIST returns a directory listing and DELE deletes a remote file.

questions.questionText: During an FTP login the server replies 331 User name okay, need password. What does the first digit 3 of an FTP reply code mean?
options: Positive completion: the requested action has been fully carried out
Transient negative: the command failed but may succeed if repeated later
Positive intermediate: the command was accepted, but another command (here PASS) is needed to complete it
Permanent negative: the command failed and should not be repeated unchanged
questions.explanation: FTP reply codes start with 1 (positive preliminary), 2 (positive completion), 3 (positive intermediate), 4 (transient negative) or 5 (permanent negative). 331 therefore asks the client to continue with PASS, after which 230 confirms the login.

questions.questionText:
An FTP session shows these lines:
C: USER alice
S: 331 Password required for alice
C: PASS summer26
S: 230 User logged in
C: PASV
S: 227 Entering Passive Mode (198,51,100,20,78,32)
C: RETR sales.csv
S: 550 sales.csv: No such file or directory
What happened?
options: The login failed, because 331 is an error reply
Alice logged in, but the download failed permanently because the requested file does not exist
The data connection could not be opened, so the client should simply retry later
The file was transferred, and 550 confirms that the transfer is complete
questions.explanation: 331 followed by 230 is a successful login, and 227 gives the passive data port. 550 is a permanent negative reply meaning the file is unavailable; a failed data connection would be 425, and a successful transfer ends with 226.

questions.questionText: An FTP client sits behind a firewall that allows only outgoing connections. In one passive-mode session it lists the remote directory once and then downloads 3 files. How many TCP connections does the client open, and to which server ports?
options: 4: one to port 21 and three to port 20
2: one to port 21 and one to port 20 that carries all the data
5: one to port 21, plus four that the server opens from its port 20
5: one to port 21 and four to the high ports announced in the server's 227 replies
questions.explanation: Every listing or file needs its own data connection, so there are 1 + (1 + 3) = 5 connections. In passive mode the client opens all of them, the data connections going to the ports given in the 227 replies, which an outbound-only firewall allows; the server connecting from port 20 would be active mode.

questions.questionText: A 30 MB file is downloaded by FTP at an average throughput of 12 Mbps. Taking 1 MB = 10^6 bytes and 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s, and ignoring set-up delays, how long does the transfer take?
questions.explanation: T = 8F / R = (30 x 10^6 x 8 bit) / (12 x 10^6 bit/s) = 240 / 12 = 20 s. Forgetting the factor 8 gives 2.5 s.

questions.questionText: A ZIP archive downloaded with a command-line FTP client from a Linux server to a Windows PC arrives corrupted, while text files transfer correctly. What is the most likely cause?
options: Passive mode was used instead of active mode
The control connection on port 21 was closed during the transfer
The transfer used ASCII mode (TYPE A), which rewrote line-ending bytes; binary mode (TYPE I) must be used for such files
The file was larger than TFTP's 512-byte block size
questions.explanation: ASCII mode converts between LF and CR LF line endings, which corrupts any byte in a binary file that happens to look like a line ending. Binary (image) mode copies every byte unchanged; active or passive mode does not change the contents.

questions.questionText: What is anonymous FTP?
options: FTP that hides the client's IP address from the server
Access to a public FTP server by logging in with the user name 'anonymous' instead of a personal account
FTP in which the password is encrypted with SSH
A mode of FTP that needs no control connection
questions.explanation: Public download servers often accept the user name anonymous (or ftp), traditionally with an e-mail address as the password, so FTP does not always need a personal account. It gives no privacy or encryption: the session is still plain text.

questions.questionText: Which statement about TFTP is correct?
options: It has no login and no directory listing, and is used mainly to boot diskless hosts and to load router or switch images and configurations
It encrypts every block with the user's SSH key
It uses a TCP control connection on port 69 and a separate data connection
It can resume an interrupted transfer from any byte offset
questions.explanation: TFTP keeps only read and write requests, 512-byte DATA blocks, ACKs and error messages over UDP, which makes it small enough for boot ROMs (PXE) and network devices. It offers no authentication, encryption or resume.

questions.questionText: A 2048-byte file is sent with TFTP using the default 512-byte blocks and no losses. How many DATA packets are sent, and how much data does the last one carry?
options: 4 packets; the last one carries 512 bytes
5 packets; the last one carries 512 bytes
4 packets; the last one carries 0 bytes
5 packets; the last one carries 0 bytes
questions.explanation: A DATA packet with fewer than 512 data bytes marks the end of the file. 2048 = 4 x 512, so after 4 full blocks the sender adds a fifth DATA packet carrying 0 bytes to signal the end.

questions.questionText: TFTP sends 512-byte blocks with stop-and-wait: each DATA block must be acknowledged before the next is sent. A 6000-byte configuration file is sent over a path with RTT = 25 ms. Ignoring transmission times, processing and the initial request, how long does the transfer take, from sending the first DATA block until the sender receives the ACK for the last one?
options: 275 ms
300 ms
150 ms
25 ms
questions.explanation: Blocks = floor(6000 / 512) + 1 = 11 full blocks + one 368-byte block = 12, and each costs one RTT: 12 x 25 ms = 300 ms. Forgetting the last partial block gives 275 ms, and charging only the one-way delay gives 150 ms.

questions.questionText: Which statement about SFTP and FTPS is correct?
options: SFTP is FTP over SSL on port 990, while FTPS runs over SSH on port 22
Both use port 21 and differ only in the cipher they choose
SFTP is an SSH subsystem that uses one connection on port 22, while FTPS is classic FTP protected by TLS, with separate control and data connections
SFTP is TFTP with encryption added, so it runs over UDP
questions.explanation: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) is not FTP at all: it runs inside an SSH connection. FTPS keeps FTP's commands and two connections and wraps them in TLS, explicitly on port 21 or implicitly on port 990.

questions.questionText: Which pairing correctly describes the two ways of running FTPS?
options: Explicit FTPS: connect to port 21 and send AUTH TLS before logging in; implicit FTPS: TLS starts at once on port 990
Explicit FTPS: TLS starts at once on port 990; implicit FTPS: connect to port 21 and send AUTH TLS
Explicit FTPS: connect to port 22 and start SSH; implicit FTPS: connect to port 21 and send STARTTLS
Explicit FTPS: the password is sent base64-encoded; implicit FTPS: the password is sent in plain text
questions.explanation: In explicit FTPS (RFC 4217) the client asks for protection on the normal control port with AUTH TLS; implicit FTPS expects a TLS handshake as soon as the client connects to port 990 (with data on 989). Base64 is only an encoding, not encryption.

questions.questionText: Both SCP and SFTP run over SSH on port 22. What does the classic SCP protocol lack compared with SFTP?
options: Encryption of the file contents
Authentication with SSH keys
The ability to copy whole directories recursively
Directory listing, resuming interrupted transfers and remote file management such as renaming and deleting
questions.explanation: SCP only copies files (recursively with -r) inside an encrypted SSH session, with the same password or key authentication. SFTP is a full file-access protocol that can also list, resume, rename and delete, which is why WinSCP and modern OpenSSH prefer it.

questions.questionText: What does the command scp -P 2222 backup.tar admin@203.0.113.9:/srv/ do?
options: Downloads /srv/backup.tar from 203.0.113.9 into the local folder
Copies the local file backup.tar to the /srv/ folder on 203.0.113.9, logging in as admin over SSH on port 2222
Copies backup.tar to the server over plain FTP on port 2222
Copies backup.tar over SSH on port 22 and sets its permissions to 2222
questions.explanation: scp copies from its first argument to its second, and user@host:path names a remote location, so this is an upload. The -P option (capital P) selects the SSH port instead of the default 22.

questions.questionText: A network engineer captures a Telnet session to a router with Wireshark. What can she read in the capture?
options: Nothing, because Telnet encrypts the session with TLS
Only the port numbers, because Telnet encrypts its payload with DES
The user name, the password and every command, all in plain text
Only the router's host-key fingerprint
questions.explanation: Telnet sends every keystroke unencrypted, so following the TCP stream in Wireshark reveals the login and all the commands. SSH encrypts the same kind of session, which is why it has replaced Telnet for remote administration.

questions.questionText: Telnet, the older unencrypted remote-login protocol, listens on which TCP port?
questions.explanation: Telnet uses TCP port 23. Port 21 is FTP control, 22 is SSH (and SFTP/SCP) and 25 is SMTP.

questions.questionText: SSH is built from three protocols. Which order is correct, from the one running directly over TCP up to the one that carries shell sessions and tunnels?
options: Transport layer protocol, then user authentication protocol, then connection protocol
User authentication protocol, then transport layer protocol, then connection protocol
Connection protocol, then transport layer protocol, then user authentication protocol
Transport layer protocol, then connection protocol, then user authentication protocol
questions.explanation: The transport layer protocol (RFC 4253) authenticates the server, exchanges keys and encrypts; the user authentication protocol (RFC 4252) then checks the password or key; and the connection protocol (RFC 4254) multiplexes channels for shells, SFTP and port forwarding.

questions.questionText: The first time PuTTY connects to a server, it shows a security alert saying the server's host key is not cached and displays the key's fingerprint. What is this check for?
options: Checking the strength of the user's password
Creating the user's own public/private key pair
Letting the user confirm the server's identity, so that a man-in-the-middle cannot pose as the server
Checking that the server's TLS certificate was issued by a trusted CA
questions.explanation: SSH authenticates the server by its host key; the user should compare the fingerprint with one obtained from the administrator. PuTTY then caches the key and warns loudly if it ever changes, which may indicate an attack.

questions.questionText: An administrator sets up key-based SSH login from PuTTY to a Linux server. Which arrangement is correct?
options: Copy the private key into the server's authorized_keys file and keep the public key on the client
Generate the key pair in PuTTYgen, add the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, and keep the passphrase-protected private key (.ppk) on the client
Send the private key to the server at each login so that the server can compare it with its stored copy
Put the public key in the server's known_hosts file and the private key in PuTTY's host-key cache
questions.explanation: The server stores only the public key; at login the client proves it holds the matching private key by signing a challenge, so the private key never leaves the client. known_hosts and PuTTY's host-key cache hold server host keys, not user keys.

questions.questionText: What does Pageant, part of the PuTTY suite, do?
options: Generates new RSA and Ed25519 key pairs
Copies files from the command line over SCP
Converts Telnet sessions into SSH sessions
Holds decrypted private keys in memory so that PuTTY and WinSCP can authenticate without asking for the passphrase every time
questions.explanation: Pageant is PuTTY's SSH authentication agent: the passphrase is typed once and later logins use the cached key. PuTTYgen generates keys, and PSCP and PSFTP are the command-line file-transfer tools.

questions.questionText: A new switch has not yet been given an IP address. How can an administrator open its command-line interface with PuTTY?
options: Select the Serial connection type and use the console cable's COM port at the device's speed, typically 9600 bit/s
Open an SSH session to the address 0.0.0.0
Open a Telnet session to the switch's MAC address
Open WinSCP in SCP mode and browse the switch's file system
questions.explanation: Without an IP address SSH and Telnet cannot reach the device, but PuTTY also drives serial lines for out-of-band console access. Cisco consoles typically use 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit.

questions.questionText: In PuTTY, a user connects by SSH to gateway.example.com and adds a local port forward with source port 8080 and destination 10.0.0.5:80. What happens when the user's browser then opens http://localhost:8080?
options: The browser connects straight to 10.0.0.5 port 80 without using SSH
gateway.example.com opens port 8080 to everyone on the Internet
PuTTY carries the connection inside the encrypted SSH session to gateway.example.com, which then connects to 10.0.0.5 port 80
PuTTY sends the request by Telnet to 10.0.0.5 on port 8080
questions.explanation: A local forward makes PuTTY listen on the client's port 8080; each connection to it is tunnelled through the SSH session, and the gateway opens the onward connection to 10.0.0.5:80. Only the hop from the gateway to 10.0.0.5 is outside the encrypted tunnel.

questions.questionText: Which list contains only protocols that WinSCP can use to transfer files?
options: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and Amazon S3
Telnet, rlogin and serial
DNS, DHCP and SNMP
questions.explanation: WinSCP is a file-transfer client: SFTP is its default protocol, and SCP, FTP (optionally with TLS), WebDAV and S3 are also supported. Interactive Telnet, rlogin and serial sessions are PuTTY's job.

subtopics.title: Electronic Mail
subtopics.subtitle: MUA, MTA and MDA; SMTP push; POP3 vs IMAP pull; MIME, webmail and email security

concepts.text: Email Architecture

Internet email has three major components: user agents, mail servers and the protocols between them. Each user has a mailbox on a mail server; each server also keeps an outgoing message queue. Sending is done with SMTP, a push protocol, while reading mail from one's own mailbox uses a pull (access) protocol such as POP3, IMAP or HTTP for webmail.
The agents involved in delivering a message:
items: MUA (Mail User Agent): the program the user reads and writes mail with, e.g. Outlook, Thunderbird, a phone mail app or a webmail page.
MTA (Mail Transfer Agent): the mail server software that relays messages between servers using SMTP, e.g. Postfix, Sendmail, Exim, Microsoft Exchange.
MDA (Mail Delivery Agent): places the arriving message into the recipient's mailbox (e.g. Dovecot LDA, procmail), from which POP3/IMAP serve it.

concepts.text: SMTP

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers mail over a persistent TCP connection, traditionally on port 25 between servers; mail clients submit mail on port 587 (with STARTTLS and authentication) or 465 (implicit TLS). It is a push protocol: the sender's server opens the connection and pushes the message. Classic SMTP requires message bodies in 7-bit ASCII, and the server replies to each command with a three-digit code such as 220 ready, 250 OK and 354 start mail input.

concepts.text: MIME
MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) lets 7-bit SMTP carry non-ASCII text, attachments and media by adding headers:
items: MIME-Version: 1.0 marks the message as MIME.
Content-Type: type/subtype such as text/plain, text/html, image/jpeg, application/pdf, multipart/mixed (several parts with a boundary), multipart/alternative.
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit, 8bit, quoted-printable (mostly-ASCII text) or base64 (binary data, 3 bytes become 4 characters).
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=... tells the MUA to offer the part as a file.

concepts.plainText: Base64 size = 4 x ceiling(n / 3) characters for n input bytes (about 33% larger)

concepts.text: Webmail (Gmail, Outlook.com) replaces POP3/IMAP between the user and the server with HTTP or HTTPS: the browser is the user agent and talks to a web front end, while the mail servers still exchange messages with each other using SMTP.
Email security in brief:
items: Transport: STARTTLS on SMTP and TLS versions of POP3/IMAP (995/993) encrypt each hop but not the stored message.
End-to-end: PGP and S/MIME sign and encrypt the message itself (covered under network security).
Sender authentication: SPF lists the IPs allowed to send for a domain and DKIM adds a domain signature checked through DNS; DMARC sets the policy for failures.

concepts.text: Worked Example: Alice Emails Bob
Message flow from alice@a.com to bob@b.com:
items: 1. Alice composes the mail in her MUA, which submits it with SMTP (port 587) to her mail server mail.a.com.
2. The message waits in mail.a.com's outgoing queue; the server looks up the MX record of b.com in DNS.
3. mail.a.com opens a TCP connection to port 25 of mail.b.com and runs HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA and QUIT.
4. The MDA at b.com stores the message in Bob's mailbox; if delivery fails, mail.a.com retries (typically every 30 minutes) and eventually bounces it.
5. Bob's MUA later pulls the message with IMAP or POP3, or Bob reads it through webmail over HTTPS.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Electronic Mail
Your notes on e-mail, cleaned up and corrected:
items: SMTP only sends: the client pushes outgoing mail to its own server, and that server pushes it on to the recipient's server. SMTP is never used to read a mailbox.

In step 2 of the sending sequence the client submits mail on port 587 (STARTTLS plus login) or 465 (implicit TLS), not on port 25; port 25 is for server-to-server relay and many ISPs block it for home users.
Step 3 needs DNS: the sending server looks up the MX record of the recipient's domain to find the server to deliver to.
Step 4 is done by the Mail Delivery Agent (MDA), which files the message into the recipient's mailbox.
POP3 (port 110, or 995 with TLS) downloads mail to one device. Deleting the server copy is the usual default, but most clients offer 'leave a copy on the server'.

IMAP (port 143, or 993 with TLS) keeps mail, folders and read/unread flags on the server, so every device sees the same mailbox. In short: POP3 = download (and usually delete), IMAP = keep on the server and synchronise.

concepts.text: SMTP keeps the envelope separate from the content. MAIL FROM and RCPT TO form the envelope that MTAs use for routing and for bounces, while From:, To:, Cc: and Subject: are header lines inside DATA that are shown to the reader, and the two need not agree. A Bcc recipient gets its own RCPT TO but is removed from the header, which is how it stays hidden. Because a line holding only a dot ends DATA, the client doubles any leading dot in the body (dot-stuffing) and the server removes the extra dot again.
Inside POP3 and IMAP sessions:
items: POP3 moves through the AUTHORIZATION state (USER, PASS), the TRANSACTION state (STAT, LIST, RETR n, DELE n, RSET, and the optional TOP n k that returns the headers plus k body lines) and the UPDATE state entered by QUIT; replies are +OK or -ERR, and messages marked with DELE are removed only in UPDATE.
IMAP commands carry a tag that the server repeats in its final reply, for example a1 LOGIN, a2 SELECT INBOX, a3 FETCH 5 (BODY[HEADER]), a4 STORE 5 +FLAGS (\Seen), a5 LOGOUT.
IMAP flags include \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged and \Deleted; EXPUNGE permanently removes the messages marked \Deleted from the selected mailbox.
IMAP IDLE keeps a mailbox selected so that the server can push new-mail notices at once instead of the client polling.
