concepts.text: Common mistakes: SMTP is not used to read mail; port 25 is for relay, while 587 and 465 are for submission; TLS on SMTP, POP3 or IMAP protects only one hop, so end-to-end secrecy needs PGP or S/MIME; base64 is an encoding, not encryption; and SPF, DKIM and DMARC authenticate the sending domain but encrypt nothing.
For base64 questions, work in groups of 3 bytes: size = 4 x ceil(n / 3), the padding is '==' when n mod 3 = 1 and '=' when n mod 3 = 2, and to go backwards from an encoded size limit multiply by 3/4.

formulas.plainText: Base64 overhead is about 33% before line breaks

notes.text: SMTP is push (sending and server-to-server relay); POP3 and IMAP are pull (reading your own mailbox). A mail client uses both: SMTP out, POP3/IMAP in.
Mail servers find the destination server through the DNS MX record of the recipient's domain, not the A record of the domain itself.
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode a base64 attachment; confidentiality needs TLS, PGP or S/MIME.

formulas.title: Base64 encoded size
formulas.description: Number of base64 characters produced from n bytes of binary data, ignoring line breaks.

formulas.title: Base64 overhead
formulas.description: Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, so encoded attachments grow by about one third.

flashcards.front: What are MUA, MTA and MDA?
flashcards.back: Mail User Agent (client program), Mail Transfer Agent (server relaying mail with SMTP) and Mail Delivery Agent (puts mail into the recipient's mailbox).

flashcards.front: Why was MIME needed?
flashcards.back: SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII text; MIME adds headers and encodings such as base64 so attachments, images and non-English text can be sent.

flashcards.front: Which SMTP command begins the message content, and how is it ended?
flashcards.back: DATA begins it (server replies 354), and a line containing a single dot ends it.

questions.questionText: A 3000-byte binary file is attached to an email using base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding. Ignoring line breaks, what is the size of the encoded attachment?
options: 3000 bytes
3750 bytes
4000 bytes
6000 bytes
questions.explanation: Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters: 4 x (3000 / 3) = 4000 bytes, about 33% larger.

questions.questionText: A mail client both sends and reads e-mail. For which tasks is SMTP used?
options: Only downloading new mail from the user's mailbox to the client
Both sending mail and reading the user's mailbox
Submitting the user's outgoing mail to the mail server and relaying it between mail servers, but not reading the user's mailbox
Only relaying between mail servers; clients submit their mail with IMAP
questions.explanation: SMTP is a push protocol: the client pushes outgoing mail to its server (submission on port 587) and servers push it on to the recipient's server (port 25). Reading one's own mailbox uses a pull protocol: POP3, IMAP, or HTTPS for webmail.

questions.questionText: Which pair of TCP ports does IMAP use, first without TLS and then with implicit TLS (IMAPS)?
questions.explanation: IMAP listens on port 143 (often upgraded with STARTTLS) and on port 993 for IMAP over implicit TLS. 110 and 995 are the POP3 equivalents, and 25 and 465 belong to SMTP.

questions.questionText: Which of these is a protocol for retrieving (downloading) e-mail from a mailbox on a mail server?
options: SMTP
ARP
FTP
POP3
questions.explanation: POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3, port 110) lets a mail client download messages from its mailbox; IMAP is the other common retrieval protocol. SMTP sends mail, ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses and FTP transfers files.

questions.questionText: Which pair of standards protects an e-mail message end to end, encrypting and signing the message itself so that even the mail servers it passes through cannot read it or change it undetected?
options: STARTTLS and SMTPS
PGP and S/MIME
SPF and DKIM
POP3S and IMAPS
questions.explanation: PGP and S/MIME encrypt the message for the recipient and sign it with the sender's key, so the protection stays with the message. STARTTLS, SMTPS, POP3S and IMAPS protect only each hop between machines, and SPF and DKIM authenticate the sending domain without encrypting anything.

questions.questionText: Which option correctly matches each program to its role in the e-mail system?
options: Thunderbird: MTA; Postfix: MDA; Dovecot LDA: MUA
Thunderbird: MDA; Postfix: MUA; Dovecot LDA: MTA
Thunderbird: MUA; Postfix: MTA; Dovecot LDA: MDA
Thunderbird: MUA; Postfix: MDA; Dovecot LDA: MTA
questions.explanation: Thunderbird is a Mail User Agent that the user reads and writes mail with; Postfix is a Mail Transfer Agent that relays mail between servers with SMTP; and Dovecot's LDA is a Mail Delivery Agent that files arriving mail into the mailbox.

questions.questionText: Many ISPs block outgoing connections to TCP port 25 from home broadband customers. Why do they do this, and how can their customers still send e-mail from a mail client?
options: To stop home PCs from receiving mail directly; customers must read their mail with IMAP instead
Because port 25 uses UDP, which home routers cannot translate; customers switch to a TCP port
To stop spam from infected home PCs; customers can then send mail only through webmail, because mail clients can no longer send
To stop malware-infected home PCs from delivering spam straight to other mail servers; customers submit mail with authentication to their provider's submission service, which relays it on port 25
questions.explanation: Port 25 is the server-to-server relay port, so blocking it from residential addresses stops botnets from sending spam directly. Mail clients authenticate to their provider's submission service (port 587 with STARTTLS or 465 with implicit TLS), and only the provider's MTA talks to other servers on port 25.

questions.questionText: A mail client's account settings show: incoming server port 995 and outgoing server port 465, both using TLS from the moment the connection opens. Which protocols does the client use?
options: POP3 over implicit TLS to read mail, and SMTP submission over implicit TLS to send it
IMAP over implicit TLS to read mail, and SMTP submission over implicit TLS to send it
POP3 over implicit TLS to read mail, and unencrypted SMTP relay to send it
IMAP with STARTTLS to read mail, and SMTP with STARTTLS to send it
questions.explanation: 995 is POP3 over TLS (IMAP over TLS would be 993), and 465 is message submission with implicit TLS (RFC 8314). STARTTLS is used on the plain ports 110, 143 and 587, and server-to-server relay uses port 25 (with opportunistic STARTTLS when both servers support it).

questions.questionText: In which order does an SMTP client issue these commands to send one message?
options: MAIL FROM, EHLO, DATA, RCPT TO, QUIT
EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT
EHLO, RCPT TO, MAIL FROM, DATA, QUIT
EHLO, DATA, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, QUIT
questions.explanation: The client first greets the server (EHLO, or HELO in basic SMTP), then gives the envelope sender with MAIL FROM and one RCPT TO per recipient, sends the content after DATA ending with a lone dot, and closes with QUIT.

questions.questionText: While delivering one message, a sending MTA receives the reply 450 (mailbox temporarily unavailable, try again later) for bob@b.com and 550 (mailbox unavailable, no such user) for bobb@b.com. What does it do?
options: Bounces both copies to the sender immediately
Retries both copies until they are delivered
Retries bobb@b.com later and bounces Bob's copy at once
Keeps Bob's copy queued and retries later, but returns a bounce (non-delivery report) to the sender for bobb@b.com at once
questions.explanation: 4xx SMTP replies are transient failures, so the MTA keeps the message queued and retries, typically for several days, before giving up. 5xx replies are permanent, so it generates the bounce straight away.

questions.questionText: Alice sends one message with To: bob@b.com, carol@b.com, Cc: dave@b.com and Bcc: erin@b.com. Her server delivers it to mail.b.com in a single SMTP session. How many RCPT TO commands are sent, and does Bob's copy show Erin's address?
options: 3; no, because Bcc copies are always sent in a separate SMTP session
4; yes, because every copy carries the full To, Cc and Bcc header lines
4; no, because a Bcc recipient appears in the envelope (RCPT TO) but not in the delivered header
1; no, because the receiving server reads the To and Cc lines to find the recipients
questions.explanation: Delivery follows the envelope: one RCPT TO per recipient (bob, carol, dave and erin, so 4) and then one DATA. The Bcc line is removed from the header before sending, so no recipient sees Erin's address.

questions.questionText: How does the SMTP envelope (MAIL FROM and RCPT TO) differ from the message's From: and To: header lines?
options: MTAs route the message and send bounces using the envelope, while the header lines are part of the content shown to the reader, so the two need not match
They are always identical, and a server rejects any message in which they differ
The header lines are used for routing, and the envelope is only displayed to the reader
The envelope is encrypted by SMTP, while the header lines travel in plain text
questions.explanation: The envelope is exchanged as SMTP commands, while the headers travel inside DATA. Because a sender can write any address in From:, forged senders are easy, which is what SPF, DKIM and DMARC try to detect.

questions.questionText: The body of a message being sent by SMTP contains a line consisting of a single dot. How does the client send that line so that the server does not end the message early?
options: It silently drops the line
It sends the line as two dots, and the receiving server removes the extra leading dot
It sends the whole body base64-encoded as a single MIME part
It sends RSET and starts the mail transaction again
questions.explanation: A line holding only '.' ends the DATA section, so SMTP uses dot-stuffing (RFC 5321): the client adds a dot to every line that starts with a dot and the server strips it off. The recipient therefore sees the original line.

questions.questionText: Which POP3 command downloads message number 2 from the mailbox?
options: FETCH 2 BODY[]
GET 2
DATA 2
RETR 2
questions.explanation: POP3 uses short commands such as USER, PASS, STAT, LIST, RETR, DELE and QUIT, and answers +OK or -ERR. FETCH belongs to IMAP, GET to HTTP and DATA to SMTP.

questions.questionText: In a POP3 session the client sends DELE 3 and receives +OK, and then the connection drops before the client sends QUIT. What happens to message 3?
options: It is deleted at the moment DELE 3 is acknowledged with +OK
It is moved to a Trash folder on the server
It stays on the server, because deletions are carried out only in the UPDATE state that begins after QUIT
It is deleted from the mailbox but kept in the server's backup copy
questions.explanation: A POP3 session passes through the AUTHORIZATION, TRANSACTION and UPDATE states. DELE only marks a message; the marks are applied when QUIT moves the session into UPDATE, so a session that ends without QUIT (or after RSET) leaves every message in place.

questions.questionText: Which capability does IMAP offer that POP3 does not?
options: Server-side folders and message flags, and fetching a single MIME part (such as one attachment) without downloading the whole message
Encrypting the session with TLS
Logging in with a user name and password
Downloading complete messages to the client
questions.explanation: IMAP treats the server as the master copy: folders, flags such as Seen and Flagged, server-side search and fetching of individual MIME parts all work there. POP3 sees a single inbox (its optional TOP command can return the headers but not a chosen part), while both protocols support TLS, password login and whole-message download.

questions.questionText:
An IMAP client sends these commands:
a1 LOGIN bob secret
a2 SELECT INBOX
a3 FETCH 5 (BODY[HEADER])
a4 STORE 5 +FLAGS (\Deleted)
a5 EXPUNGE
What has happened to message 5 by the end of the session?
options: The whole message was downloaded and deleted from the client only
Its headers were read, it was flagged for deletion and it was then permanently removed from the INBOX
It was moved into a folder named Deleted
It was forwarded to another user
questions.explanation: FETCH 5 (BODY[HEADER]) returns only the header section, STORE +FLAGS (\Deleted) marks the message, and EXPUNGE permanently removes every message marked \Deleted from the selected mailbox. Each command carries a tag (a1, a2, ...) that the server repeats in its reply.

questions.questionText: How can an IMAP client be told about new mail immediately, without polling the server every few minutes?
options: It sends RCPT TO with its own address
It sends the POP3 command UIDL in a loop
It issues the IDLE command, keeping the connection open so that the server can push notices of new messages
It publishes an MX record pointing at itself
questions.explanation: IMAP IDLE (RFC 2177) keeps a selected mailbox open; the server sends untagged EXISTS responses as mail arrives, and the client ends the wait with DONE. RCPT TO and MX records belong to delivery, and UIDL still needs polling.

questions.questionText: Why can a JPEG photo not be placed directly, as raw bytes, in the body of a classic SMTP message?
options: SMTP limits every message to 64 KB
SMTP runs over UDP, which loses large messages
JPEG files must be encrypted before any network transfer
Classic SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII text in lines of limited length, so binary data must first be encoded, for example with base64
questions.explanation: SMTP was designed for 7-bit US-ASCII lines of at most 1000 characters, so arbitrary bytes would be damaged or rejected. MIME adds Content-Type and Content-Transfer-Encoding headers so that the image can travel as base64 text.

questions.questionText: Which MIME header tells the receiving mail client that the message has several parts, such as a text body and an attached PDF?
options: Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="XyZ"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Disposition: inline
questions.explanation: A multipart Content-Type declares several body parts separated by the boundary string, each with its own headers. Content-Transfer-Encoding says how one part is encoded, MIME-Version marks the message as MIME, and Content-Disposition says whether a part is shown inline or as an attachment.

questions.questionText: A newsletter carries the same content twice, as a text/plain part and a text/html part, so that each mail client displays the best version it supports. Which Content-Type encloses the two parts?
options: multipart/mixed
multipart/related
multipart/alternative
message/rfc822
questions.explanation: In multipart/alternative every part is a version of the same content, from simplest to richest, and the client shows the richest one it can display. multipart/mixed holds independent parts such as attachments, multipart/related ties an HTML part to its inline images, and message/rfc822 encloses a whole forwarded message.

questions.questionText: A 100-byte binary attachment is base64-encoded. Ignoring line breaks, how many characters does the encoding contain, and how many of them are '=' padding characters?
options: 134 characters, no padding
136 characters, 2 of them '='
136 characters, 1 of them '='
133 characters, no padding
questions.explanation: Output = 4 x ceil(100 / 3) = 4 x 34 = 136 characters. Since 100 = 33 x 3 + 1, the last group holds a single byte, which becomes two data characters followed by '=='.

questions.questionText: What is the base64 encoding of the two ASCII characters Hi (bytes 0x48 0x69)?
options: SGk
SGk==
SGkA
SGk=
questions.explanation: The 16 bits 01001000 01101001 are padded with two zero bits and split into the 6-bit groups 010010, 000110 and 100100 = 18, 6 and 36, which are S, G and k. Only 2 bytes of the 3-byte group were present, so one '=' completes the 4-character block.

questions.questionText: A 5700-byte file is base64-encoded and split into lines of 76 characters, each line (including the last) followed by CRLF. What is the total size of the encoded data?
options: 7800 bytes
7600 bytes
7700 bytes
11,400 bytes
questions.explanation: Characters = 4 x ceil(5700 / 3) = 7600, which fill 7600 / 76 = 100 lines; each line adds 2 bytes of CRLF, so the total is 7600 + 200 = 7800 bytes, about 37% more than the original.

questions.questionText: A mail provider limits each message to 25 MB after encoding. Ignoring headers and line breaks, what is the largest binary file that can be sent as a base64 attachment?
options: 25 MB
questions.explanation: Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters, so the raw file can be at most 25 x 3 / 4 = 18.75 MB. Multiplying by 4/3 instead gives 33.33 MB, and simply taking 33% off the limit gives 16.75 MB.

questions.questionText: In quoted-printable Content-Transfer-Encoding, how is the byte 0xE9 (the letter é in ISO-8859-1) written?
options: \xE9
questions.explanation: Quoted-printable leaves most printable ASCII characters unchanged and writes any other byte as '=' followed by two hexadecimal digits, so 0xE9 becomes =E9. %E9 is URL percent-encoding, \xE9 is a programming-language escape and é is an HTML character reference.

questions.questionText: Which statement about MIME is NOT correct?
options: The header MIME-Version: 1.0 marks a message as using MIME
Quoted-printable suits text that is mostly ASCII with a few special characters
Base64 encoding keeps an attachment confidential, because it cannot be decoded without a key
In a multipart message the parts are separated by a boundary string declared in Content-Type
questions.explanation: Base64 is a public, reversible encoding that anyone can decode, so confidentiality needs TLS, PGP or S/MIME. The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: What does a domain's SPF record, published in DNS, let a receiving mail server check?
options: Whether the message body has been changed since the sending domain signed it
Whether the IP address of the connecting server is authorised to send mail for the domain used in the envelope sender (MAIL FROM)
Which host accepts incoming mail for the domain
Whether the recipient's mailbox exists before the message is sent
questions.explanation: An SPF TXT record such as v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.0/24 include:_spf.example.net -all lists the permitted senders, and the receiver compares the connecting IP address with it. Body signatures are DKIM's job, and the host that accepts incoming mail is named by the MX record.

questions.questionText: How does DKIM let a receiving server verify a message?
options: The sending domain signs selected header fields and the body with its private key, and the receiver checks the signature with the public key published in a DNS TXT record at selector._domainkey.domain
The sender encrypts the message with the recipient's public key, so only the recipient can decrypt it
The receiver compares the connecting server's IP address with a list of permitted senders in DNS
The receiver opens a second SMTP connection to the sending server and asks it to confirm the message
questions.explanation: A DKIM-Signature header names the signing domain (d=) and selector (s=); the receiver fetches the key from DNS and verifies the signature, showing that the message passed through that domain unchanged. Checking the connecting IP is SPF, and encrypting for the recipient is PGP or S/MIME.

questions.questionText: A domain publishes the DNS record v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com. A message with From: ceo@example.com arrives, and neither SPF nor DKIM passes in alignment with example.com. What should the receiver do, and what does DMARC add to SPF and DKIM?
options: Deliver it to the inbox, because DMARC only produces reports
Deliver it to the spam folder, because p=reject means quarantine
Encrypt it before delivery, because DMARC is an encryption standard
Reject the message; DMARC ties the SPF and DKIM results to the visible From: domain, states the policy for failures and requests aggregate reports
questions.explanation: DMARC passes only if SPF or DKIM passes for a domain aligned with the From: header. With p=reject a failing message should be refused, p=quarantine sends it to spam and p=none only monitors, while rua gives the address for aggregate reports.

questions.questionText: A user reads and sends mail through a webmail site in a browser. Which protocols are involved?
options: IMAP between the browser and the webmail server, with no SMTP at all
POP3 from the browser to download mail, and SMTP from the browser on port 25 to send it
HTTPS between the browser and the webmail server, and SMTP between the provider's mail servers and other mail servers
FTP to download each message as a file
questions.explanation: With webmail the browser is the user agent and talks HTTP over TLS to the web front end, which reads the mailbox itself. Messages to and from other domains still travel between mail servers by SMTP.

subtopics.title: DNS & Peer-to-Peer Applications
subtopics.subtitle: DNS hierarchy, resolution, records and caching; P2P models, BitTorrent, distribution time

concepts.text: Domain Name System

DNS maps human-friendly host names such as www.example.com to IP addresses, and also provides host aliasing, mail-server lookup and load distribution across replicated servers. It is a distributed, hierarchical database implemented by many name servers, plus an application-layer protocol by which hosts query it. A single central DNS server would be a single point of failure, too heavily loaded and too far from most users, so the database is split across the hierarchy.
The hierarchical name space, read from right to left:
items: Root: the unnamed top of the tree, served by 13 root-server identities (a to m) replicated worldwide with anycast.
Top-level domains (TLD): generic (.com, .org, .net, .edu) and country-code (.np, .uk, .in) servers.
Second-level domains: names registered under a TLD, e.g. example.com or tu.edu.np; further labels form subdomains, e.g. www.example.com.
Each label is up to 63 characters and a full name up to 253 characters.

concepts.text: The name space is divided into zones, each administered separately. An authoritative name server holds the definitive records for its zone; a primary (master) server holds the editable copy and secondary (slave) servers copy it by zone transfer, which uses TCP. The local DNS server (resolver) of an ISP or organisation receives queries from hosts and resolves them on their behalf.

rows: Contacted server returns a referral to the next server
Contacted server finds the full answer itself
Low on root and TLD servers
Heavy on the server doing the recursion
Local resolver querying root, TLD and authoritative servers
Host (stub resolver) querying its local DNS server
Local server makes separate queries to each level
Query and answer pass down and back up a chain
Domain to mail server, with preference
Zone to its authoritative name server
Primary server, admin, serial, refresh, TTL
Free text, used for SPF, DKIM, verification

concepts.text: Caching, transport and security:
items: Every resolver caches answers for the record's TTL (time to live, in seconds); caching of TLD server addresses means root servers are rarely contacted.
DNS uses port 53: UDP for ordinary queries (classic 512-byte limit, extended by EDNS0), TCP for zone transfers and large responses.
Reverse lookup finds the name for an IP using PTR records under in-addr.arpa (IPv4) or ip6.arpa (IPv6), with the address octets reversed.
Security: plain DNS is open to cache poisoning and spoofing; DNSSEC adds signatures, and DoH/DoT encrypt queries.

concepts.text: Peer-to-Peer Applications

rows: Always-on server, clients never talk directly
Every peer is both client and server
Server has a fixed, well-known IP
Peers join and leave, IPs change
Self-scaling: new peers add upload capacity
Hard to manage, secure and make reliable

concepts.text: Unstructured vs structured P2P overlays:
items: Unstructured (Gnutella): peers connect arbitrarily; a query is flooded to neighbours with a TTL limit. Simple and robust but generates heavy traffic and may miss rare files.
Hybrid (original Napster, KaZaA super-peers): a central or super-peer index answers searches while files move directly between peers.

Structured (DHT): a distributed hash table assigns each key to the peer whose ID is closest; Chord arranges peers on a ring and finds any key in O(log N) hops using finger tables. Kademlia is used by BitTorrent's trackerless mode.

concepts.text: BitTorrent in outline:
items: A torrent is the set of peers sharing one file; the file is divided into chunks (commonly 256 KB).
A tracker (or DHT) tells a joining peer the addresses of other peers; seeds hold the complete file, leechers are still downloading.
Rarest-first: a peer requests the chunks fewest neighbours hold, spreading rare chunks quickly.
Tit-for-tat: a peer uploads to the four peers sending to it fastest (re-evaluated every 10 s) and optimistically unchokes one random peer every 30 s.

concepts.plainText: Client-server distribution time D_cs >= max(NF / u_s, F / d_min)
P2P distribution time D_p2p >= max(F / u_s, F / d_min, NF / (u_s + sum of peer uploads))

concepts.text: To send a file of F bits to N peers, a server with upload rate u_s must push N copies itself, so client-server distribution time grows linearly with N. In P2P, the server need upload only one copy and each peer re-uploads chunks, so total upload capacity grows with N and distribution time levels off. For example, with F = 100 Mb, u_s = 20 Mbps and d_min = 10 Mbps, 10 clients need max(50 s, 10 s) = 50 s under client-server.
Going Deeper: DNS & P2P
Your DNS notes, cleaned up and completed:
items: DNS (port 53) exists because people remember names such as www.google.com, while IP routing works only with numeric addresses such as 142.250.190.46; DNS translates between the two.

In the simple four-step flow, the browser really asks the operating system's stub resolver, which checks its own cache and hosts file and then sends one recursive query to the configured local DNS server (the ISP's or organisation's resolver, or a public one such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8).

The local server answers from its cache when it can; otherwise it works down the hierarchy itself: a root server, then the TLD server (.com), then the authoritative server for google.com, which holds the actual A record.
Every answer is cached for its TTL, so most lookups never reach the root or TLD servers.

DNS mainly uses UDP because a query and its answer are each one small message, so no connection set-up is needed; it switches to TCP port 53 for zone transfers and for answers too large for one UDP message.

Besides name-to-address mapping, DNS gives host aliasing (CNAME), mail-server lookup (MX), reverse lookup (PTR) and load distribution by returning several A records in rotating order (round-robin DNS).

concepts.text:
Worked trace 1: host h resolves www.example.com, all caches empty
1  h     -> local  query www.example.com A   (recursive, RD = 1)
2  local -> root   same query                 (iterative)
3  root  -> local  referral: .com NS records + their addresses (glue)
4  local -> TLD    same query
5  TLD   -> local  referral: example.com NS ns1.example.com + glue A
6  local -> auth   same query
7  auth  -> local  answer 203.0.113.10, TTL 3600, AA = 1
8  local -> h      answer; local server caches every record it learned
Total: 4 queries + 4 replies = 8 messages (a fully recursive chain also uses 8)
Next lookup of ftp.example.com: example.com NS is cached, so only 2 pairs = 4 messages

rows: Matches a reply to its query; chosen at random by the asker
Set when the answer comes from an authoritative server, not a cache
Reply was truncated; repeat the query over TCP
Recursion desired (by the asker) / recursion available (at the server)
0 NOERROR, 2 SERVFAIL, 3 NXDOMAIN (no such name), 5 REFUSED
Numbers of question, answer, authority and additional records

concepts.plainText: Remaining TTL of a cached record = original TTL - (time now - time it was cached); the record is discarded at 0

concepts.text: Several record rules come up again and again. An MX record carries a preference number, and a sending server tries the lowest value first, falling back to higher values only if that server cannot be reached; equal values share the load. A CNAME may not coexist with any other record at the same name, so it cannot be placed at the zone apex (example.com), which must hold the SOA and NS records. When a zone's name server lies inside the zone it serves, such as ns1.example.com for example.com, the parent's referral must carry that server's address as a glue record, or no resolver could ever reach it.
Reverse lookups, zone transfers and security:
items: Reverse lookup writes the address backwards under in-addr.arpa: 203.0.113.25 becomes 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa, queried for a PTR record. IPv6 uses ip6.arpa with all 32 hexadecimal digits (nibbles) reversed, one label each.

A secondary server fetches the primary's SOA every refresh interval (every retry interval after a failure) and runs a zone transfer over TCP (AXFR full, IXFR incremental) only when the serial number has increased; if the primary stays unreachable for the expire time, it stops answering for the zone.
The SOA minimum field sets how long 'no such name' (NXDOMAIN) answers may be cached, called negative caching.
Cache poisoning: an off-path attacker races the real answer with forged replies, so resolvers randomise both the 16-bit query ID and the UDP source port to make guessing expensive.

DNSSEC signs each record set (RRSIG) with the zone's key (DNSKEY), and the parent vouches for that key with a DS record, forming a chain of trust from the root; it gives authenticity and integrity, not secrecy.
DNS over TLS (DoT, TCP port 853) and DNS over HTTPS (DoH, port 443) encrypt the queries between a host and its resolver, hiding the names from on-path observers.

concepts.text: Your P2P notes, cleaned up and corrected:
items: Client-server: an always-on server with a fixed address stores the files and every client downloads from it, so the server's upload capacity is shared by all clients and becomes the bottleneck as their number grows.

P2P: every peer is both client and server and pieces move directly between users. A pure P2P system has no central server, but many practical systems keep one for coordination only, such as a BitTorrent tracker or the original Napster index.

More users do not make the network itself faster: each new peer adds upload capacity as well as demand, so the total distribution time grows very slowly instead of linearly, and each peer is still limited by its own download rate.

Examples: BitTorrent (file distribution), early Skype (a P2P overlay with super-nodes, later replaced by Microsoft-run servers), IPFS, and blockchain networks such as Bitcoin, where every full node stores and relays the ledger.

Advantages: self-scaling capacity, no single point of failure when peer discovery is decentralised (DHT), low cost for the content owner. Disadvantages: peers come and go (churn) and sit behind NAT, trust and security problems (malware, fake content), copyright infringement, and little central control.

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: F = 1 Gbit = 1000 Mb, u_s = 50 Mbps, every peer u = 5 Mbps, d_min = 10 Mbps
(1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s, fluid model, overheads ignored)
N = 10:    D_cs  = max(10 x 1000/50, 1000/10)            = max(200, 100)       = 200 s
           D_p2p = max(1000/50, 1000/10, 10 x 1000/(50 + 50))  = max(20, 100, 100) = 100 s
N = 100:   D_cs  = max(100 x 1000/50, 100)               = 2000 s
           D_p2p = max(20, 100, 100 x 1000/(50 + 500))   = max(20, 100, 181.8) = 181.8 s
N = 1000:  D_cs  = 20,000 s     D_p2p = max(20, 100, 10^6/5050) = 198.0 s
As N grows: D_cs rises by 20 s per peer, D_p2p creeps up towards F/u = 1000/5 = 200 s

concepts.plainText: With every peer uploading at u, as N grows D_p2p approaches max(F / u_s, F / d_min, F / u)

concepts.text: BitTorrent and DHT mechanics:
items: Joining: the .torrent file or magnet link gives the info-hash that names the torrent; the peer asks the tracker (or the DHT) for a list of peers and opens TCP connections to a subset of them.
Pieces: a 1 GiB file with 256 KiB pieces has 2^30 / 2^18 = 4096 pieces, each checked against its hash (SHA-1 in BitTorrent v1, SHA-256 in v2), so corrupted or fake pieces are rejected.

Rarest first: request the missing piece held by the fewest neighbours. Tit-for-tat: every 10 s upload to the four neighbours sending fastest, and every 30 s optimistically unchoke one random extra neighbour so newcomers can start and better partners are found.
Chord DHT: each key is stored at its successor, the first peer ID at or after the key going round the ID ring (wrapping past 0); finger tables cut a lookup from about N/2 hops to O(log2 N) hops.
BitTorrent's trackerless mode uses the Kademlia DHT, in which the distance between two IDs is their bitwise XOR.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: counting only the 4 queries when a question asks for all messages (8) in a cold iterative lookup; thinking a root server returns the IP address (it returns a referral); taking the highest MX preference as the most preferred (the lowest wins); forgetting to reverse the octets in an in-addr.arpa name; expecting P2P distribution time to fall to zero as peers join (it levels off near F/u); and assuming DNSSEC encrypts queries (it only signs data, while DoT and DoH encrypt).

formulas.plainText: D_p2p >= max(F / u_s, F / d_min, NF / (u_s + sum u_i))
Cold iterative lookup time = local + root + TLD + authoritative RTTs

DNS normally uses UDP port 53 for queries but switches to TCP port 53 for zone transfers and responses too large for UDP.
In a recursive query the contacted server does the work; in an iterative query it only returns a referral. The host to local-server query is usually recursive, the rest iterative.

flashcards.front: What does the TTL of a DNS record control?
flashcards.back: How many seconds resolvers may cache the record before they must query the authoritative server again.

flashcards.front: Which DNS record is used for reverse lookup?
flashcards.back: PTR, stored under in-addr.arpa (IPv4) or ip6.arpa (IPv6) with the address written in reverse order.

flashcards.front: What is tit-for-tat in BitTorrent?
flashcards.back: A peer uploads mainly to the peers that upload to it fastest, plus one optimistically unchoked random peer, which rewards cooperation.

flashcards.front: How does a structured P2P network such as Chord locate a key?
flashcards.back: Through a distributed hash table: peers and keys share an ID ring and finger tables let a query reach the responsible peer in O(log N) hops.

questions.questionText: A sending mail server needs to find which host accepts mail for the domain b.com. Which DNS resource record does it query?
options: CNAME
MX
PTR
SOA
questions.explanation: The MX record maps a domain to its mail server(s) with a preference value; CNAME is an alias, PTR is reverse lookup and SOA holds zone parameters.

questions.questionText: A server with upload rate 20 Mbps must distribute a 100 Mb file to 10 clients whose minimum download rate is 10 Mbps. What is the minimum distribution time in the client-server model?
options: 5 s

questions.questionText: DNS servers listen for queries on which well-known port number?
questions.explanation: DNS uses port 53, over UDP for ordinary queries and over TCP for zone transfers and large responses. Port 25 is SMTP, 80 is HTTP and 110 is POP3.

questions.questionText: Which type of DNS resource record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?
options: A record
MX record
PTR record
TXT record
questions.explanation: An A record holds an IPv4 address (AAAA holds an IPv6 address). MX names a mail server, PTR maps an address back to a name, and TXT carries free text such as SPF policies.

questions.questionText: Which DNS server holds the original, definitive records for the zone example.com, as opposed to copies cached from earlier lookups?
options: A root name server
A .com top-level-domain (TLD) server
An authoritative name server for example.com
The ISP's local (recursive) DNS server
questions.explanation: The authoritative servers (primary and secondaries) of a zone hold its records and set the AA flag in their answers. Root and TLD servers only refer resolvers downward, and the local resolver answers from its cache.

questions.questionText: A local DNS server with an empty cache sends the query for www.example.com to a root server. What does the root server send back?
options: The IP address of www.example.com
A referral giving the names and addresses of the .com TLD servers
An NXDOMAIN error, because root servers know only top-level names
A referral straight to the authoritative server for example.com
questions.explanation: Root servers know only the delegations of the top-level domains, so they answer with the NS records (plus glue addresses) of the .com servers. The .com server then refers the resolver to example.com's authoritative server, which gives the address.

questions.questionText: A host sends a recursive query for www.example.com to its local DNS server, whose cache is empty. The local server resolves the name with iterative queries to a root server, a .com TLD server and the authoritative server for example.com. How many DNS messages, queries and replies together, are sent in total?
questions.explanation: There are four query-reply pairs: host-local, local-root, local-TLD and local-authoritative, so 4 queries + 4 replies = 8 messages. The answer 4 counts only the queries.

questions.questionText: Starting with all caches empty, a host resolves www.example.com and, one minute later, ftp.example.com. The host sends recursive queries to its local DNS server, which uses iterative queries, and all TTLs are far longer than one minute. How many DNS messages (queries plus replies) do the two lookups need in total?
questions.explanation: The first lookup takes 8 messages. For the second, the local server already has example.com's NS and glue records cached from the TLD referral, so only the host-local and local-authoritative pairs are needed: 8 + 4 = 12. 14 assumes only the .com servers were cached, and 16 ignores caching.

questions.questionText: Each host's RTT to the local DNS server is 4 ms. The local server's RTTs to a root server, a .com TLD server and the authoritative server for example.com are 60 ms, 40 ms and 30 ms. With all caches empty, host A resolves www.example.com; shortly afterwards, well within the TTL, host B on the same LAN resolves the same name through the same local server. Ignoring processing time, how long does each lookup take?
options: A: 134 ms, B: 4 ms
A: 130 ms, B: 0 ms
A: 134 ms, B: 34 ms
A: 268 ms, B: 8 ms
questions.explanation: A's lookup needs the host-local RTT plus the three iterative RTTs: 4 + 60 + 40 + 30 = 134 ms. B's query is answered from the local server's cache, so it costs only the 4 ms host-local RTT.

questions.questionText: At 10:00:00 a local DNS server caches an A record that the authoritative server returned with a TTL of 3600 s. At 10:45:00 a client asks the local server for the same name. What happens?
options: It queries the authoritative server again, because cached records must be refreshed on every request
It answers from its cache with a TTL of 3600 s
It answers from its cache with a TTL of 2700 s
It answers from its cache with a TTL of 900 s
questions.explanation: 45 minutes = 2700 s have passed, so the record is still valid and is served from the cache with its remaining lifetime: 3600 - 2700 = 900 s. The cached copy is discarded only when its TTL reaches 0.

questions.questionText: Which statement about recursive and iterative DNS queries is correct?
options: In a recursive query the server asked must return the final answer or an error, doing any further lookups itself; in an iterative query it may return a referral to another server
In an iterative query each server passes the query on to the next server and relays the answer back
Root and TLD servers normally accept recursive queries from any host, which keeps resolution fast
A host's stub resolver normally sends iterative queries to the root servers itself
questions.explanation: A recursive query hands the whole job to the server asked, which is how a stub resolver uses its local DNS server. Root and TLD servers refuse recursion to limit their load and answer with referrals, which the local server follows iteratively.

questions.questionText: The domain example.org publishes three MX records: 10 mx1.example.org, 20 mx2.example.org and 30 mx3.example.org. How does a sending mail server use them?
options: It tries mx3 first, because the highest preference value wins, and then mx2
It picks one of the three at random for every message, ignoring the numbers
It sends a copy of the message to all three servers
It tries mx1 first and falls back to mx2 and then mx3 only if the better servers cannot be reached
questions.explanation: Lower MX preference values are preferred (RFC 5321), so mx1 (10) is tried first and mx2 (20) and mx3 (30) are backups. Only records with equal values are chosen between at random to share the load.

questions.questionText: A company wants shop.example.com to be an alias for shop-lb.cdnprovider.net, so that the CDN can change its server addresses without the company editing its own zone. Which record should the company create?
options: A
PTR
CNAME
NS
questions.explanation: A CNAME record makes shop.example.com an alias whose canonical name is shop-lb.cdnprovider.net, and resolvers then look up that name's A or AAAA records. An A record would fix the IP address inside the company's own zone.

questions.questionText: The .com TLD servers delegate example.com to the name server ns1.example.com. Why must their referral also contain the IP address of ns1.example.com (a glue record)?
options: Because referrals from TLD servers must always be signed with DNSSEC
Because an NS record may not point to a name outside the .com zone
So that the resolver can skip the authoritative server and cache the final answer directly
Without it a resolver would have to ask ns1.example.com for its own address, which it cannot do without that address
questions.explanation: The name server's name lies inside the zone it serves, so finding its address would mean querying that same server, a circular dependency. The parent therefore adds its A (and AAAA) record to the additional section of the referral.

questions.questionText: An administrator runs a reverse lookup on the IPv4 address 203.0.113.25. Which DNS name and record type does the resolver query?
options: 203.0.113.25.in-addr.arpa, type A
25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa, type PTR
203.0.113.25.in-addr.arpa, type PTR
25.113.0.203.ip6.arpa, type PTR
questions.explanation: Reverse names list the octets backwards, most specific first, under in-addr.arpa, so the query is for the PTR record at 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa. ip6.arpa is used only for IPv6 addresses.

questions.questionText: How does a secondary name server decide when to copy the zone from its primary server?
options: It transfers the whole zone each time a client sends it a query
The primary pushes every changed record to it over UDP port 53 as soon as it is edited, without any serial number
It checks the TTL of each record and copies the records whose TTL has expired
It fetches the SOA record every refresh interval and runs a zone transfer (AXFR or IXFR over TCP) only when the primary's serial number is higher than its own
questions.explanation: The SOA serial number is the zone's version: a secondary checks it each refresh interval (or when the primary sends a NOTIFY) and transfers the zone over TCP only if it has increased. If it cannot reach the primary for the expire time, it stops answering for the zone.

questions.questionText: A cloud e-mail provider asks the administrator of example.com to prove that she controls the domain by publishing a random token string in DNS. Which record type is normally used for such a token?
options: MX
TXT
SOA
PTR
questions.explanation: TXT records hold arbitrary text, so they carry ownership-verification tokens as well as SPF, DKIM and DMARC policies. MX names mail servers, SOA holds zone parameters and PTR is for reverse lookup.

questions.questionText: What does DNSSEC add to DNS?
options: Digital signatures on record sets (RRSIG), checked with the zone's DNSKEY and a chain of DS records from the root, so that a resolver can detect forged or altered answers
Encryption of queries and answers, so that an eavesdropper cannot see which names a user looks up
A switch from UDP to TCP for every query, which prevents spoofing
Hiding the IP addresses of authoritative servers from resolvers
questions.explanation: DNSSEC provides origin authentication and integrity: each zone signs its data and its parent vouches for its key with a DS record. It gives no confidentiality; DoT and DoH are what encrypt the queries.

questions.questionText: Which statement about DNS over TLS (DoT) and DNS over HTTPS (DoH) is correct?
options: Both sign the records at the authoritative server and so replace DNSSEC
DoT runs on UDP port 53 and DoH on TCP port 53
DoT uses its own port, TCP 853, while DoH carries DNS messages inside HTTPS on port 443, where they look like ordinary web traffic
Both encrypt the whole path from the host to the authoritative server, including the resolver's queries to root and TLD servers
questions.explanation: DoT (RFC 7858) and DoH (RFC 8484) encrypt the hop between a client and its resolver; DoT on its dedicated port is easy to recognise and block, while DoH on 443 blends in with HTTPS. Neither proves that the data is genuine, which is DNSSEC's job.

questions.questionText: An off-path attacker trying to poison a resolver's cache must forge a reply whose 16-bit transaction ID and destination UDP port both match the resolver's outstanding query. The resolver picks the ID at random and its source port at random from 16,384 ports. How many (ID, port) combinations must the attacker cover to be certain of a match?
questions.explanation: The two random values are independent, so the possibilities multiply: 2^16 x 2^14 = 2^30 = 1,073,741,824. With a fixed source port only 65,536 IDs would have to be tried, and adding the two counts (81,920) is the classic mistake.

questions.questionText:
dig www.example.org prints this answer section:

www.example.org.      300  IN  CNAME  web.cdn-example.net.
web.cdn-example.net.   60  IN  A      198.51.100.7

Which statement is correct?
options: www.example.org has two IPv4 addresses, 300 and 60
www.example.org is an alias of web.cdn-example.net, whose IPv4 address 198.51.100.7 may be cached for at most 60 s
web.cdn-example.net is an alias of www.example.org, and both records may be cached for 300 s
198.51.100.7 is the address of the DNS server that sent the answer, valid for 300 s
questions.explanation: The CNAME line says that www.example.org is an alias whose canonical name is web.cdn-example.net, and the A line gives that name's IPv4 address. The second column is the TTL in seconds: 60 s for the address and 300 s for the alias.

questions.questionText: A popular site publishes several A records for www.site.example, and its DNS server rotates their order in each reply. What is this used for?
options: Reverse lookup of the site's addresses
Encrypting DNS answers
Transferring the zone to secondary servers
Spreading client load across several replicated web servers
questions.explanation: Clients usually connect to the first address in the list, so rotating the order (round-robin DNS) spreads requests across the replicated servers. It is a simple form of load distribution without health checks.

questions.questionText: Which of the following applications is built on a peer-to-peer architecture?
options: BitTorrent file sharing
Browsing a website over HTTP
Sending mail through an SMTP server
Downloading from an FTP server
questions.explanation: In BitTorrent the peers upload pieces of the file to one another, so each is both client and server. Web, mail and FTP are client-server: clients talk only to an always-on server.

questions.questionText: Which statement about P2P file distribution is NOT correct?
options: Each new peer adds upload capacity as well as demand
Peers may leave at any time and often change IP addresses, so the system must cope with churn
The original server must upload one complete copy of the file to every peer
A peer's download time is still limited by its own download rate
questions.explanation: In P2P the server needs to send each bit only once (at least F bits in total), and the peers redistribute the pieces among themselves. Sending N full copies is the client-server case, which makes D_cs grow as NF/u_s.

questions.questionText: A server with upload rate u_s = 40 Mbps must deliver a 2 Gbit file (F = 2000 Mb) to N = 50 peers. Every peer can upload at 4 Mbps and the slowest peer downloads at 8 Mbps. Using the distribution-time bounds of Kurose and Ross (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s), what are the minimum distribution times for client-server and for P2P?
options: 2500 s and about 417 s
2500 s and 250 s
50 s and about 417 s
2500 s and 500 s

questions.questionText: In a P2P distribution every peer uploads at u = 1 Mbps, the server uploads at u_s = 10 Mbps, every peer downloads at 20 Mbps and the file is F = 600 Mb. As the number of peers N becomes very large, what happens to the minimum distribution times?
options: Both D_p2p and D_cs grow in proportion to N
D_p2p levels off at 60 s (F/u_s), while D_cs keeps growing
D_p2p falls towards 0 s, because each new peer adds capacity
D_p2p levels off just below 600 s (F/u), while D_cs keeps growing as N x 60 s
questions.explanation: D_p2p = max(F/u_s, F/d_min, NF/(u_s + Nu)) = max(60, 30, 600N/(10 + N)), and 600N/(10 + N) approaches F/u = 600 s from below. D_cs = max(NF/u_s, F/d_min) = 60N s, which grows without limit.

questions.questionText: What is the role of the tracker in BitTorrent?
options: It stores the complete file and serves it to every peer
It keeps track of the peers taking part in a torrent and gives a joining peer the addresses of some of them
It decides which piece each peer must download next
It encrypts the pieces exchanged between peers
questions.explanation: The tracker only coordinates: peers register with it and receive a list of other peers, then exchange pieces directly. Each peer chooses its own piece order (rarest first), and trackerless torrents use a DHT instead.

questions.questionText: A BitTorrent peer still needs pieces 2, 5, 7 and 9. Among its neighbours, piece 2 is held by 6 peers, piece 5 by 2, piece 7 by 9 and piece 9 by 4. Under the rarest-first policy, which piece does it request first?
options: Piece 2
Piece 7
Piece 9
Piece 5
questions.explanation: Rarest first requests the missing piece held by the fewest neighbours, here piece 5 with 2 copies. This spreads scarce pieces quickly and makes it less likely that a piece disappears when peers leave.

questions.questionText: Alice's neighbours are currently sending her data at these rates (kbit/s): B 150, C 60, D 90, E 200, F 40 and G 110. Under BitTorrent's tit-for-tat policy, which neighbours does Alice unchoke as her four regular upload partners?
options: E, B, G and D
B, C, D and E
E, B, G and C
C, F, D and G
questions.explanation: Every 10 s Alice uploads to the four neighbours sending to her fastest: E (200), B (150), G (110) and D (90). Separately, every 30 s she optimistically unchokes one more random neighbour, such as C or F, so that new peers can start and faster partners can be found.

questions.questionText: A 1.5 GiB file (1.5 x 2^30 bytes) is shared by BitTorrent in 256 KiB (2^18-byte) pieces. How many pieces does the torrent contain?
questions.explanation: 1.5 x 2^30 / 2^18 = 1.5 x 2^12 = 6144 pieces. Taking 1 GiB as 1000 MiB gives 6000, and counting bits instead of bytes gives 49,152.

questions.questionText: In a Chord DHT with 1,024 peers, every peer keeps a finger table. On the order of how many peers must a lookup contact in the worst case?
options: About 512
About 10
About 32
questions.explanation: Each finger-table hop at least halves the remaining distance round the ring, so a lookup needs O(log2 N) = log2 1024 = 10 hops. Following successor pointers alone would take up to N - 1 = 1,023 hops (N/2 on average).

questions.questionText: A Chord ring uses 4-bit identifiers (0 to 15) and has peers with IDs 1, 4, 9, 11 and 14. Each key is stored at its successor, the first peer whose ID is equal to or follows the key going clockwise. Which peers store keys 12 and 15?
options: 11 and 14
14 and 14
11 and 1
14 and 1
questions.explanation: Key 12: the first peer ID at or after 12 is 14. Key 15: no peer ID is 15 or above, so the search wraps past 0 to peer 1.

subtopics.title: Socket Programming & Application Servers
subtopics.subtitle: Socket API calls for TCP and UDP, echo server and client in C, and application servers

concepts.text: The Socket API

A socket is the interface (a door) between an application process and the transport layer, created and controlled through an API such as Berkeley sockets (Unix) or Winsock (Windows). A process names its socket with an IP address and a port number. A stream socket (SOCK_STREAM) uses TCP and gives a reliable byte stream after a connection is set up; a datagram socket (SOCK_DGRAM) uses UDP and sends independent messages, each with a destination address; a raw socket (SOCK_RAW) accesses IP directly.

rows: Create an endpoint; returns a descriptor
Attach a local IP address and port
Mark the socket passive and set the backlog queue
Block until a client connects; returns a new connected socket
Start the TCP three-way handshake to the server
Write and read data on the connected socket
Release the socket; TCP sends FIN

concepts.text: UDP socket sequence (no connection, no listen or accept):
items: Server: socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0), bind() to a known port, then loop on recvfrom(), which also returns the sender's address, and reply with sendto().
Client: socket(), then sendto() with the server address in every call, recvfrom() for the reply, and close().
Each datagram is independent; the application must handle loss, duplication and ordering itself.

concepts.text: Server Design
Blocking vs non-blocking sockets:
items: Blocking (default): accept(), recv() and connect() suspend the process until the operation can complete. Simple, but one slow client stalls an iterative server.
Non-blocking: set with fcntl(O_NONBLOCK) or ioctlsocket(); calls return immediately with EWOULDBLOCK/EAGAIN if they cannot proceed, so the program must poll or use event notification.

concepts.text: Ways to build a concurrent server that serves many clients at once:
items: Process per client: fork() after accept(); the child handles the connection while the parent returns to accept().
Thread per client or a thread pool: cheaper than processes, sharing memory with the need for synchronisation.
I/O multiplexing: select(), poll() or epoll/kqueue let one thread watch many sockets and serve whichever is ready (event-driven, as in Nginx and Node.js).

concepts.text: Different CPUs store multi-byte integers differently (x86 is little-endian), while network protocols use big-endian network byte order. Port numbers and addresses placed in socket structures must therefore be converted with htons() and htonl() (host to network, short 16-bit and long 32-bit) and back with ntohs() and ntohl(). inet_pton() and inet_ntop() convert between text addresses and binary form.

concepts.plainText: A 16-bit port field gives 2^16 = 65536 ports, numbered 0 to 65535

concepts.text: Application Servers

A web server (Apache HTTP Server, Nginx) mainly accepts HTTP requests and returns static content, passing dynamic requests on. An application server hosts the business logic of an application and generates dynamic content, providing middleware services such as database connection pooling, transactions, security, session management and messaging. Middleware is the software layer between the operating system and applications that hides distribution details from programmers.

rows: User interface, displays data and takes input
Tomcat, JBoss/WildFly, IIS with ASP.NET, Node.js

concepts.text: Well-known servers:
items: Apache Tomcat: Java servlet and JSP container.
JBoss / WildFly (Red Hat): full Java EE / Jakarta EE application server; others include Oracle WebLogic and IBM WebSphere.
Microsoft IIS: web server that hosts ASP.NET applications on Windows.
Node.js: JavaScript runtime with an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, often used with the Express framework.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Sockets & Servers
Your socket notes, cleaned up and made precise:
items: A socket is one endpoint of a communication channel, named by an IP address, a port and a transport protocol. Socket programming means writing network applications on this API, in C (Berkeley sockets, Winsock on Windows), Python (the socket module), Java (Socket, ServerSocket, DatagramSocket) and most other languages.
'Server creates socket and listens' is really three calls: socket(), bind() to a known port and listen(); the server then waits in accept().
'Client creates socket and connects': socket() and connect(); a client normally does not call bind(), because the operating system picks an ephemeral port.
'Data exchanged': send() and recv() on the connected socket that accept() returned, never on the listening socket.
'Close connection': close() makes TCP send a FIN, and the peer's recv() then returns 0 (b'' in Python), which is how it detects the end of the data.
UDP needs none of listen(), accept() or connect(): the server binds a port and both sides use sendto() and recvfrom() with explicit addresses.

concepts.text:
import socket, threading

def handle(conn, addr):
    with conn:
        while data := conn.recv(1024):     # b'' means the client closed
            conn.sendall(data)             # loops until every byte is sent

srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 7000))
srv.listen(5)                              # up to 5 connections queued
while True:
    conn, addr = srv.accept()              # new socket + client (IP, port)
    threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(conn, addr)).start()

import socket
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9999))              # no listen() or accept()
cli = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
cli.sendto(b"ping", ("127.0.0.1", 9999))   # address given in every call
data, addr = srv.recvfrom(2048)            # one whole datagram + sender
srv.sendto(data.upper(), addr)
print(cli.recvfrom(2048))                  # (b'PING', ('127.0.0.1', 9999))

rows: connect() on the client, listen() and accept() on the server
None; the first sendto() already carries data
Byte stream with no message boundaries
Lost data retransmitted and delivered in order
May be lost, duplicated or reordered
One listening socket plus one per client

concepts.text: accept() takes the oldest connection from the listen queue and returns a new socket for it together with the client's address, a (host, port) tuple in Python, while the listening socket stays open for further clients. The kernel, not the application, completes the three-way handshake, so a client's connect() succeeds as soon as its connection is queued, even before the server calls accept(). The backlog argument of listen() limits how many such connections may wait; when the queue is full, new attempts are held off or refused, depending on the operating system. On a TCP socket send() may take fewer bytes than requested and returns the number it took, so programs loop or use Python's sendall().

Worked example 1: byte order on a little-endian (x86) host
Port 5000 = 0x1388; network byte order (big-endian) sends the high byte first: 13 88
htons(5000) returns 0x8813, which the CPU stores in memory as 13 88, so the wire carries 13 88
Bug: sin_port = 5000 without htons() -> memory 88 13 -> the network reads 0x8813 = 34835
Address 10.0.0.200 -> 0A 00 00 C8 on the wire (inet_pton() writes it in network order)
A TCP header starting 00 50 C3 51 -> source port 0x0050 = 80, destination 0xC351 = 50001
Rule: a port read from the wire = 256 x first byte + second byte

concepts.plainText: n clients arriving together at an iterative server that needs S seconds each: the k-th finishes at kS, so the average completion time is (n + 1) S / 2

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 5 clients arrive together at t = 0, each needs S = 2 s of service
Iterative server: clients finish at 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 s
  average completion = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 5 = 6 s = (5 + 1) x 2 / 2
Concurrent server, work mostly waiting on disk or network (I/O-bound):
  the five handlers overlap and all finish at about 2 s
Concurrent server, each request needs 2 s of CPU on a single core:
  the threads share the CPU and all five finish at about 10 s,
  so concurrency helps responsiveness only when the bottleneck is not the CPU
Application servers and the servers they sit beside:
items: Your note is right: an application server is middleware between the client and the database. It runs the business logic, while the database stores the data and the browser or app displays it.

Node.js is a JavaScript runtime rather than an application server; application servers are built on it (for example with Express) and serve many clients from one thread with a non-blocking event loop.

Web servers (Apache HTTP Server, Nginx, IIS) serve static files, terminate TLS and pass dynamic requests to the application server; mail servers run SMTP, IMAP and POP3; DNS servers answer on port 53; DHCP servers answer broadcasts on UDP port 67; file servers share folders with SMB (TCP 445) or NFS (2049).

An iterative server handles one client at a time, which suits short UDP request-reply exchanges; a concurrent server handles many at once (process, thread or event per client) and is the norm for TCP services such as web, mail and file servers.
In a fork() server (above) the child closes the listening socket and the parent closes the connected one, so each process holds only what it needs and closed connections really close.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: forgetting htons() on the port, so the server listens on a byte-swapped port; calling recv() on the listening socket instead of the socket accept() returned; assuming that one send() arrives as one recv() on TCP (it is a byte stream, so read until a whole message is in); ignoring the return value of send(); treating recv() returning 0 as an error instead of the peer's orderly close; and calling listen() or accept() on a UDP socket.

formulas.plainText: A connection is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol

notes.text: Server order: socket, bind, listen, accept, recv/send, close. Client order: socket, connect, send/recv, close. UDP drops listen, accept and connect and uses sendto/recvfrom.
accept() returns a new socket for the client; the original listening socket keeps waiting for further connections. Reading from the listening socket is a common bug.
Ports 0 to 1023 are well-known, 1024 to 49151 registered, and 49152 to 65535 dynamic (ephemeral) ports given to clients.

formulas.title: Port number space
formulas.description: TCP and UDP port fields are 16 bits wide, giving port numbers 0 to 65535.

formulas.title: Connection identifier
formulas.plainText: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol)
formulas.description: The five-tuple that uniquely identifies each connection, letting one server port serve many clients.

flashcards.front: What does listen() do in a TCP server?
flashcards.back: It turns the bound socket into a passive listening socket and sets the backlog of pending connections waiting for accept().

flashcards.front: Why are htons() and htonl() needed?
flashcards.back: They convert 16-bit and 32-bit values from host byte order to big-endian network byte order before placing them in socket structures.

flashcards.front: How does an application server differ from a web server?
flashcards.back: A web server mainly serves static HTTP content; an application server runs business logic and provides middleware such as transactions, pooling and sessions.

questions.questionText: In a TCP server, which socket call blocks until a client completes a connection and returns a new socket descriptor for that client?
options: listen()
bind()
accept()
connect()
questions.explanation: accept() takes a completed connection from the listen queue and returns a new connected socket; listen() only marks the socket passive.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the htons() function in socket programming?
options: Convert a 16-bit value from host byte order to network byte order
Convert a host name into an IP address
Convert a 32-bit address from network to host byte order
Set a socket to non-blocking mode
questions.explanation: htons means host to network short: it converts 16-bit values such as port numbers to big-endian network byte order.

questions.questionText: Which pair of calls is used to exchange data on a connectionless UDP socket without calling connect()?
options: listen() and accept()
sendto() and recvfrom()
send() and recv() only
read() and bind()
questions.explanation: UDP sockets usually use sendto(), which carries the destination address, and recvfrom(), which reports the sender's address; there is no listen or accept.

questions.questionText: In a three-tier web application, which of the following typically runs in the middle (application) tier?
options: A web browser
A MySQL database server
A DNS root server
Apache Tomcat
questions.explanation: Tomcat is an application server hosting business logic in the middle tier; the browser is presentation and MySQL is the data tier.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of socket programming in networking?
options: To let two programs, usually on different devices, communicate over a network through endpoints called sockets
To encrypt the packets sent over a network
To convert MAC addresses into IP addresses
To compress HTTP responses
questions.explanation: Socket programming writes network applications with the socket API: each side creates a socket (IP address and port) and exchanges data through it over TCP or UDP. Encryption is the job of TLS, and address mapping belongs to ARP and RARP.

questions.questionText: What is the primary role of an application server in a multi-tier system?
options: To store the DNS records of a domain
To run the application's business logic as middleware between client programs and the database
To route packets between networks
To encrypt e-mail messages
questions.explanation: An application server such as Tomcat or WildFly sits in the middle tier: it takes client requests, applies the business rules, reads and writes the database and returns the results. DNS servers hold DNS records and routers forward packets.

questions.questionText: Which socket type gives an application a reliable, connection-oriented byte stream?
options: SOCK_DGRAM
SOCK_RAW
SOCK_STREAM
AF_INET
questions.explanation: In the Internet family SOCK_STREAM sockets use TCP and deliver an ordered, reliable byte stream after a connection is set up. SOCK_DGRAM uses UDP, SOCK_RAW gives direct access to IP, and AF_INET is the address family, not a socket type.

questions.questionText: What is network byte order?
options: Big-endian: the most significant byte of a multi-byte value is sent first
Little-endian: the least significant byte is sent first
Whatever byte order the sending host's CPU uses
A byte order that the two hosts agree on when the connection is set up
questions.explanation: Internet protocols carry multi-byte fields such as ports and addresses big-endian, whatever the CPU. Little-endian hosts such as x86 PCs therefore convert with htons()/htonl() before sending and ntohs()/ntohl() after receiving.

questions.questionText: In a Python TCP server, the statement conn, addr = srv.accept() has just returned. What is addr?
options: The server's own IP address and listening port
The MAC address of the client's network card
The number of connections still waiting in the listen queue
The client's IP address and port number, as a (host, port) tuple
questions.explanation: accept() returns a new socket (conn) for the connection and the address of the connecting client, for example ('192.0.2.7', 51544). The server's own address is given by conn.getsockname().

questions.questionText: Windows PCs map a network drive to a shared folder on a company file server. Which protocol and port do they normally use?
options: NFS on port 2049
SMB on TCP port 445
FTP on TCP port 21
SMTP on TCP port 25
questions.explanation: Windows file and printer sharing uses SMB (CIFS), today directly over TCP port 445. NFS (port 2049) is the usual Unix and Linux file-sharing protocol, and FTP copies whole files rather than mounting a drive.

questions.questionText: What does the select() call let a single-threaded server do?
options: Choose the fastest route to each client
Select the strongest cipher suite for a TLS connection
Wait on many sockets at once and find out which are ready to read or write, so that it can serve many clients without a thread per client
Pick a free ephemeral port for an outgoing connection
questions.explanation: select() (and its successors poll() and epoll or kqueue) blocks until at least one socket in a set is readable or writable and reports which ones. This I/O multiplexing is the basis of event-driven servers.

questions.questionText: Traditionally, the ping program sends its ICMP Echo Request messages through which kind of socket?
options: A raw socket (SOCK_RAW), because ICMP runs directly over IP and has no port numbers
A stream socket (SOCK_STREAM) connected to TCP port 7
A UDP datagram socket sending to port 7, the echo service
A SOCK_SEQPACKET socket
questions.explanation: ICMP messages are carried directly in IP datagrams (protocol number 1) with no transport header, so ping builds them on a raw socket, which normally needs administrator rights. Port 7 belongs to the separate TCP/UDP echo service.

questions.questionText:
What does this Python program print?

import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
c = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
c.sendto(b"hello", s.getsockname())
c.sendto(b"world!", s.getsockname())
d1, _ = s.recvfrom(1024)
d2, _ = s.recvfrom(1024)
print(d1, d2)
options: b'helloworld!' b''
b'hello' b'hello'
Nothing: the program blocks, because recvfrom() needs connect() first
b'hello' b'world!'
questions.explanation: UDP keeps message boundaries: each sendto() becomes one datagram and each recvfrom() returns exactly one whole datagram, so d1 and d2 are the two messages. Merging them into one read would be TCP byte-stream behaviour.

questions.questionText:
What does this Python program print?

import socket
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
srv.listen()
c = socket.create_connection(srv.getsockname())
conn, addr = srv.accept()
c.sendall(b"hi")
c.close()
print(conn.recv(10), conn.recv(10))
options: b'hi' and then a ConnectionResetError
b'hi' b''
b'hi' b'hi'
Only b'hi', because the second recv() blocks for ever waiting for more data
questions.explanation: The first recv() returns the 2 bytes sent. After the client's close() (a FIN), recv() returns an empty bytes object, the signal of an orderly end of stream (0 in C); it would block only if the connection were still open with no data.

questions.questionText: A client has sent its whole request over TCP and wants to tell the server that no more data is coming, while still reading the server's reply on the same socket. Which call does it use?
options: close(s), after which the client can still read the reply
listen(s, 0), which marks the socket as finished
shutdown(s, SHUT_WR), which sends a FIN for the client's sending direction only
send(s, "", 0, 0), which sends an empty segment that the server reads as the end of data
questions.explanation: shutdown() with SHUT_WR half-closes the connection: the server's recv() returns 0 after the request, yet the client can still receive the reply. close() releases the socket in both directions, and a zero-length send() transmits nothing.

questions.questionText: A TCP server calls listen(s, 5) but is slow to call accept(). What does the value 5 control?
options: The maximum number of connections the kernel holds in the queue waiting for accept(); beyond that, new connection attempts are held off or refused
The maximum number of clients the server can ever serve
The number of seconds listen() waits for a client before returning
The number of bytes each client may send before accept() is called
questions.explanation: The backlog limits the queue of connections that the kernel has set up but the application has not yet accepted. When it is full, Linux simply ignores new SYNs so that clients retry, while other systems may refuse them with a RST.

questions.questionText: A programmer calls listen() on a UDP (SOCK_DGRAM) socket. What happens?
options: The socket starts accepting UDP connections, one per client
The call succeeds and makes recvfrom() return only datagrams from the first sender
The socket is silently switched to TCP
The call fails with an 'operation not supported' error, because listen() and accept() apply only to connection-oriented sockets
questions.explanation: UDP has no connections to queue, so listen() on a datagram socket fails (EOPNOTSUPP on Linux, WSAEOPNOTSUPP 10045 on Windows). A UDP server simply binds its port and loops on recvfrom().

questions.questionText: A UDP client calls connect() on its datagram socket before sending. Which statement is correct?
options: A three-way handshake is carried out with the server
No packet is sent; connect() only records a default peer, so the client can use send() and recv(), and datagrams from other addresses are filtered out
connect() fails, because UDP sockets cannot be connected
The server must call accept() for the connect() to complete
questions.explanation: For UDP, connect() is a purely local operation that fixes the destination and filters incoming datagrams; it also lets ICMP 'port unreachable' errors be reported on the socket. Only TCP's connect() starts a handshake.

questions.questionText: A program calls send() on a TCP socket to send a 4,000-byte buffer, and send() returns 1,200. What does this mean, and what should the program do?
options: 1,200 bytes were lost, and TCP will retransmit them later on its own
The receiver has already read 1,200 bytes, so nothing more is needed
Only the first 1,200 bytes were accepted; it must call send() again for the remaining 2,800 bytes, or use a loop such as Python's sendall()
The connection has failed, because send() must take all of the data or none
questions.explanation: send() returns how many bytes it copied into the kernel's send buffer, which can be fewer than requested. The program continues from byte 1,201, sending 4,000 - 1,200 = 2,800 more bytes.

questions.questionText: On an ordinary blocking TCP socket, which of these calls does NOT wait for anything from the network?
options: accept(), when no client has connected yet
recv(), when no data has arrived
connect(), until the handshake completes
listen()
questions.explanation: listen() only marks the socket as passive and sets the backlog, and returns at once. accept() waits for a client, recv() for data and connect() for the three-way handshake to finish.

questions.questionText: On a little-endian x86 PC, a C server sets addr.sin_port = 8080 without calling htons(), then binds and listens. To which port must clients really connect to reach it?
options: None, because bind() fails with an error
questions.explanation: 8080 = 0x1F90, which a little-endian CPU stores as the bytes 90 1F. The network reads sin_port big-endian, so the server really listens on 0x901F = 36895; htons(8080) would have stored 1F 90.

options: 12 34, on every host
34 12, on every host
12 34 on a big-endian host, but 34 12 on a little-endian host
34 12 on a big-endian host, but 12 34 on a little-endian host
questions.explanation: htons() returns the value arranged so that its bytes in memory are in network (big-endian) order, so the first byte is always 0x12. A big-endian host's htons() changes nothing, while a little-endian host's swaps the bytes to reach the same memory layout.

questions.questionText: In what order are the four bytes of the IPv4 address 192.168.1.10 carried in an IP header (network byte order)?
questions.explanation: Each decimal octet becomes one byte, 192 = C0, 168 = A8, 1 = 01 and 10 = 0A, and the most significant (leftmost) byte goes first. 0A 01 A8 C0 is the little-endian memory order of the same 32-bit value.

questions.questionText: An iterative TCP server takes 3 s to serve each request. Four clients connect at the same moment, t = 0, and are served one after another; set-up time is negligible. When does the last client finish, and what is the average completion time?
options: 3 s; 3 s
questions.explanation: The clients finish at 3, 6, 9 and 12 s, so the last finishes at 12 s and the average is (3 + 6 + 9 + 12) / 4 = 7.5 s = (n + 1)S/2. Everyone finishing at 3 s would need a concurrent server whose handlers overlap.

questions.questionText: In a concurrent TCP server that calls fork() after each accept(), both processes then hold the listening socket and the new connected socket. Which descriptors should each process close?
options: The child closes the listening socket and serves the client; the parent closes the connected socket and goes back to accept()
The parent closes the listening socket, and the child closes the connected socket
Neither closes anything, because the two processes share a single descriptor
Both close the listening socket, and the child reopens it when it finishes
questions.explanation: Each process keeps only what it needs: the child talks to its client and the parent accepts new ones. If the parent kept the connected socket open, the connection would not close when the child finished, and descriptors would leak.

options: Its connect() fails at once with 'connection refused'
Its connect() succeeds because the kernel queues the connection, but it gets no echo until A closes and the loop returns to accept()
It is echoed at once, because recv() switches between clients automatically
Its message is echoed to client A instead
questions.explanation: The kernel completes B's handshake and holds the connection in the listen queue (backlog 5), so connect() returns. The server, however, is stuck in the inner recv() loop for A and calls accept() for B only after A's recv() returns 0.

questions.questionText: Which statement best distinguishes a web server such as Nginx from an application server such as Apache Tomcat?
options: The web server runs only on port 443, while the application server runs only on port 80
The application server stores the data permanently, replacing the database
The web server works at the network layer, while the application server works at the transport layer
