The web server mainly serves static files and passes other requests on, while the application server runs the business logic that builds dynamic responses, with services such as database connection pooling and transactions
questions.explanation: Front-end web servers handle HTTP, TLS, static content and reverse proxying, while application servers such as Tomcat, WildFly or a Node.js app execute application code. Both work at the application layer, and the database tier still stores the data.

questions.questionText: In the classic design of servers, which pairing is usual?
options: UDP servers are usually concurrent with a separate socket per client, and TCP servers are usually iterative
Both kinds must be iterative, because a socket can serve only one client at a time
Connectionless (UDP) servers are usually iterative, handling one datagram at a time on one socket; connection-oriented (TCP) servers are usually concurrent
Both kinds must be concurrent, because an iterative server cannot call accept()
questions.explanation: A UDP request is usually one short datagram, so a single loop of recvfrom(), processing and sendto() serves clients quickly in turn. A TCP client may hold its connection for a long time, so TCP servers give each connection its own process, thread or event handler.

questions.questionText: Why is a DHCP server built on UDP rather than TCP?
options: A client that has no IP address yet can only broadcast from 0.0.0.0, and TCP cannot set up a connection by broadcast
UDP encrypts the address being assigned
TCP cannot use port numbers below 1024
DHCP messages are too large to fit in TCP segments
questions.explanation: TCP needs a connection between two unicast addresses, which a client without an address cannot have. DHCP therefore uses UDP broadcasts (client port 68, server port 67), and a relay agent forwards them across routers.

questions.questionText: Which statement about TCP server sockets is NOT correct?
options: A server needs one listening socket plus one connected socket for each client it is serving
A single server process can hold connected sockets for many clients at the same time
recv() on a connected socket returns 0 when the client has closed its side of the connection
After accept() returns, the listening socket cannot accept other clients until the new connection has been closed
questions.explanation: The listening socket keeps listening after each accept(), and new clients queue on it while earlier ones are served, which is what makes concurrent servers possible. The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: A hex dump of a TCP segment begins with the bytes 1F 90 00 50. What are the segment's source and destination ports?
options: Source 36895, destination 20480
Source 8080, destination 80
Source 80, destination 8080
Source 8080, destination 50
questions.explanation: The TCP header starts with the 16-bit source port and then the 16-bit destination port, both big-endian: 0x1F90 = 8080 and 0x0050 = 80. Reading the bytes little-endian gives 36895 and 20480, and 50 treats the hex digits as decimal.

questions.questionText:
What does this Python program print?

import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
s.settimeout(0.5)
try:
    data, addr = s.recvfrom(1024)
    print("got", data)
except socket.timeout:
    print("timed out")
options: got b'' at once, because no datagram is waiting
Nothing: recvfrom() blocks for ever
timed out, after about 0.5 s
An error at once, because a UDP socket must call connect() before recvfrom()
questions.explanation: No datagram ever arrives, so the normally blocking recvfrom() waits; settimeout(0.5) limits the wait and raises socket.timeout (TimeoutError) after 0.5 s. Without the timeout the call would block indefinitely.

questions.questionText: How does a Node.js server handle many client connections at the same time?
options: By starting a new operating-system process for every request
By serving one client completely before accepting the next
By opening a separate listening port for each client
With a single-threaded event loop and non-blocking I/O, running a callback whenever a socket is ready
questions.explanation: Node.js registers its sockets with the operating system's event mechanism (epoll, kqueue or IOCP, through libuv) and runs JavaScript callbacks as events occur, so one thread serves thousands of connections. CPU-heavy work in a callback therefore stalls every client.

questions.questionText: On Linux, a TCP server with several active client connections is stopped and restarted at once. The restarted server's bind() to port 8000 fails with 'Address already in use', although no process is listening on that port. What is the cause, and what is the usual fix?
options: Connections from the old server are still in TIME_WAIT on port 8000; setting SO_REUSEADDR on the new socket before bind() lets it bind
The clients still hold port 8000 open; the fix is to restart the clients
The kernel keeps a closed listening socket for 2 MSL; the fix is to call listen() with a backlog of 0
A port that has been used once can never be used again; the fix is to choose a new port each time
questions.explanation: Stopping the server closes its connections from the server side first (active close), so they wait in TIME_WAIT for 2 MSL with local port 8000. SO_REUSEADDR allows a listening socket to bind to a port that has only such lingering connections.

subtopics.title: Traffic Analysers: MRTG, PRTG, SNMP, Packet Tracer & Wireshark
subtopics.subtitle: Network monitoring with SNMP, MRTG and PRTG graphs, Packet Tracer simulation and Wireshark

concepts.text: Why Monitor a Network
Network monitoring and management goals (the ISO FCAPS model):
items: Fault management: detect, locate and fix failures of links and devices.
Configuration management: track and change device settings and inventory.
Accounting: measure usage per user or department for billing and quotas.
Performance: watch utilisation, delay, loss and throughput to plan capacity and find bottlenecks.
Security: detect unusual traffic, attacks and unauthorised access.

concepts.text: SNMP

The Simple Network Management Protocol lets a manager (network management station) query and control agents running on routers, switches, servers and printers. Each agent exposes a MIB (Management Information Base), a database of managed objects defined in SMI/ASN.1. Every object is named by an OID (object identifier), a dotted path in a global tree, e.g. 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5 (sysName) or ifInOctets under 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10. SNMP runs over UDP: agents listen on port 161 for requests and managers receive traps on port 162.

rows: Read the value of one or more OIDs
Read the next OID, used to walk a table
Read many OIDs in one request
Change a value, e.g. shut an interface
Unsolicited alert (link down, reboot), not acknowledged

concepts.plainText: Utilisation = 8 x change in octet counter / (interval x interface speed) x 100%

concepts.text: MRTG and PRTG
MRTG (Multi Router Traffic Grapher):
items: Free, open-source tool (Perl and C) that polls routers and switches with SNMP, by default every 5 minutes, reading interface octet counters.
Draws daily, weekly, monthly and yearly traffic graphs of inbound and outbound rates as web pages (PNG images plus HTML).
Can graph any SNMP counter or script output (CPU, temperature); RRDtool and front ends such as Cacti grew out of it.

concepts.text: PRTG Network Monitor (Paessler):
items: Commercial Windows-based monitoring suite, free for up to 100 sensors.
A sensor is one measured value, e.g. bandwidth of one port, ping time, disk space or HTTP response time.
Collects data through SNMP, WMI, packet sniffing, NetFlow/sFlow and HTTP; offers auto-discovery, maps, dashboards and alerts by email or SMS.

concepts.text: Cisco Packet Tracer

Packet Tracer is Cisco's network simulation tool used for teaching and CCNA practice. Users drag routers, switches, PCs and servers onto a workspace, cable them and configure them through a Cisco IOS command line or GUI. Real-time mode behaves like a live network, while simulation mode steps through events so each packet can be watched hop by hop with its OSI layer details. It simulates devices; it does not capture traffic from a real network.
Wireshark and tcpdump
Wireshark is a free, open-source packet analyser with a GUI:
items: Captures frames from an interface (in promiscuous or monitor mode, using libpcap/Npcap) and decodes hundreds of protocols layer by layer.
Capture filters use BPF syntax and decide what is recorded, e.g. host 192.168.1.10, port 80, tcp and not port 22.
Display filters hide or show packets already captured, e.g. ip.addr == 192.168.1.10, tcp.port == 80, http.request, dns, tcp.flags.syn == 1.
Follow TCP Stream reassembles one conversation into readable text; Statistics menus give conversations, protocol hierarchy and I/O graphs.
tcpdump is the command-line equivalent on Unix/Linux, e.g. tcpdump -i eth0 port 53 -w dns.pcap; its pcap files open in Wireshark.

rows: Reading and setting device counters, receiving traps
Designing and learning networks without hardware
Inspecting individual packets and troubleshooting protocols

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Monitoring Tools
Your monitoring notes, cleaned up and corrected:
items: MRTG (Multi Router Traffic Grapher) monitors link traffic by polling SNMP counters and graphing the average bandwidth used, which shows congestion and growth trends; it does not capture or decode packets.

PRTG, originally 'Paessler Router Traffic Grapher' and now PRTG Network Monitor, is a full monitoring suite: bandwidth, uptime (ping, HTTP), device health and alerts, viewed through a web interface or mobile apps.

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is how these tools collect the information: a manager polls the agents on routers, switches and servers, and the agents report errors and events on their own with traps.

Wireshark captures packets and decodes them layer by layer for troubleshooting. It really does show passwords sent by unencrypted protocols such as Telnet, FTP or HTTP, but not the contents of TLS or SSH sessions without their keys.
Packet Tracer is Cisco's simulator for building and testing networks without real hardware; it cannot monitor or capture traffic on a real network.

concepts.text: SNMP in more depth:
items: OID tree: iso(1).org(3).dod(6).internet(1) = 1.3.6.1; below it mgmt(2).mib-2(1) = 1.3.6.1.2.1 holds the standard MIB-II groups (system .1, interfaces .2, ip .4, tcp .6, udp .7), and private(4).enterprises(1) = 1.3.6.1.4.1 holds vendor MIBs, e.g. Cisco's under 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.
Instances: a scalar object is read with the suffix .0, e.g. sysUpTime.0 = 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0, while a table column takes the row index, e.g. ifOutOctets of interface 2 = 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.16.2.
GetBulk (v2c and v3) with N non-repeaters, R repeating variables and max-repetitions M returns up to N + M x R variable bindings in one response.

SNMP runs over UDP because each poll is one small request and reply, the manager handles timeouts and retries itself, and a connectionless protocol keeps working when the network is congested or failing.

Security: v1 and v2c authenticate only with a community string sent in clear text (the common defaults 'public' for read and 'private' for read-write are widely known); SNMPv3's User-based Security Model offers the levels noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv (HMAC authentication) and authPriv (authentication plus AES or DES encryption), with view-based access control.

concepts.text:
Trace: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.0.2.1 ifDescr   (GetNext requests to UDP 161)
GetNext ifDescr     -> ifDescr.1 = "Gi0/0"
GetNext ifDescr.1   -> ifDescr.2 = "Gi0/1"
GetNext ifDescr.2   -> ifDescr.3 = "Null0"
GetNext ifDescr.3   -> ifType.1 = 6   (outside ifDescr, so the walk stops)
A column of r rows needs r + 1 GetNext requests; here 3 + 1 = 4

rows: Traffic to or from one host

concepts.plainText: Counter increase allowing for one wrap of a 32-bit counter: delta = (C2 - C1 + 2^32) mod 2^32; rate in bit/s = 8 x delta / interval

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 32-bit ifInOctets polled 300 s apart (MRTG's default interval)
Reading 1: C1 = 4,290,000,000      Reading 2: C2 = 3,032,704   (C2 < C1, so it wrapped)
Delta = 2^32 - C1 + C2 = 4,294,967,296 - 4,290,000,000 + 3,032,704 = 8,000,000 octets
Rate  = 8 x 8,000,000 / 300 = 213,333 bit/s, about 213 kbit/s
Naive C2 - C1 = -4,286,967,296: a negative, meaningless rate
On a 2 Mbps link this is 213,333 / 2,000,000 = about 10.7 % utilisation

Worked example 2: how often must a 32-bit octet counter be polled?
Wrap time at full load = 2^32 x 8 / link rate
  100 Mbps: 34,359,738,368 / 10^8 = 343.6 s   (just longer than a 300 s poll)
  1 Gbps:   34.4 s, so it can wrap several times between 5-minute polls
Fix: the 64-bit ifHCInOctets / ifHCOutOctets counters (SNMPv2c or v3), which take
  2^64 x 8 / 10^10 = about 468 years to wrap even at 10 Gbps
Utilisation: 5,625,000 octets in 300 s on a 1 Mbps link
  = 8 x 5,625,000 / 300 = 150,000 bit/s = 15 %
Wireshark and tcpdump in practice:
items: Promiscuous mode makes the network card pass up every frame it receives, not only those addressed to it. On a switched LAN that is still only your own traffic plus broadcast, multicast and flooded frames, so seeing other hosts needs a SPAN (port-mirroring) port or a network tap; capturing all 802.11 frames on Wi-Fi needs monitor mode.
Follow TCP Stream applies the display filter tcp.stream eq N and shows the reassembled payload of that one connection, with client and server data in different colours.

Colouring rules are display filters that paint matching rows in the packet list; the default 'Bad TCP' rule, for example, highlights retransmissions, duplicate ACKs and zero windows. They never change what is captured.
Statistics menus give Conversations and Endpoints (who talks to whom, and how much), Protocol Hierarchy and I/O Graphs, and Analyze > Expert Information lists warnings such as retransmissions.
tcpdump options: -i interface, -n no name resolution, -c packet count, -w write a pcap file, -r read one, followed by a BPF expression, e.g. tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w web.pcap tcp port 80.

concepts.text: NetFlow, PRTG and Packet Tracer:
items: NetFlow (Cisco; standardised as IPFIX) makes a router group packets into flows by key fields (source and destination IP and port, protocol, ToS and input interface) and export one record per flow, with packet and byte counts and times, to a collector over UDP. It answers who is using the bandwidth, which interface counters cannot; sFlow instead samples 1 in N packets.

PRTG: each sensor is one measurement (traffic on one port, ping time, CPU load, free disk space). Data come from SNMP, WMI (Windows performance data without SNMP), packet sniffing, NetFlow/sFlow/IPFIX and HTTP, with scanning intervals from 30 s up to a day; the free edition covers 100 sensors.

Packet Tracer: Realtime mode behaves like a live network, while Simulation mode pauses time so you can step through the Event List and open each PDU to see its OSI-layer details; topologies are saved as .pkt files.

rows: How busy was the WAN link each day this month?
Long-term averages of interface octet counters
Which hosts and applications use that bandwidth?
NetFlow, sFlow or IPFIX collector (e.g. a PRTG flow sensor)
Per-flow records name the addresses and ports
Why does this one TCP connection stall?
Shows every segment, retransmission and window
Tell me at once when a link goes down
SNMP traps or informs sent to the manager
The agent reports the event without being polled
Will this OSPF design work before we buy routers?
Simulates the devices and their IOS configuration

concepts.text: MRTG and PRTG answer 'how much?' over time from SNMP counters, NetFlow answers 'who and what?', Wireshark and tcpdump answer 'what exactly is in the packets?', and Packet Tracer only simulates. Remember UDP 161 for the agent and 162 for traps, community strings in clear text for v1 and v2c, rate = 8 x change in octets / interval, and that tcp port 80 is capture syntax while tcp.port == 80 is display syntax.

formulas.plainText: Link utilisation from two SNMP counter readings
MRTG 5-minute polling gives 86400 / 300 = 288 samples per day

notes.text: SNMP ports: 161 for requests to the agent, 162 for traps to the manager, both UDP. Only SNMPv3 provides authentication and encryption.
Wireshark capture filters (BPF, e.g. port 80) and display filters (e.g. tcp.port == 80) use different syntax; typing one in the other's box fails.
MRTG and PRTG measure how much traffic flows over time using SNMP counters; Wireshark shows what is inside individual packets. Packet Tracer simulates a network rather than measuring a real one.

formulas.title: Link utilisation from SNMP
formulas.plainText: U = 8 x delta octets / (delta t x ifSpeed) x 100%
formulas.description: Percentage utilisation of an interface computed from two readings of its ifInOctets or ifOutOctets counter.

formulas.title: Samples per day
formulas.description: Number of polling samples a monitor collects per day; MRTG's 300 s interval gives 288.

formulas.title: Measured throughput
formulas.description: Average bit rate from B captured bytes over a capture interval of t seconds, as shown in Wireshark statistics.

flashcards.front: What is a MIB in SNMP?
flashcards.back: The Management Information Base: the collection of managed objects on an agent, each named by an OID, that the manager can read or set.

flashcards.front: Which SNMP version adds authentication and encryption?
flashcards.back: SNMPv3, through its user-based security model; v1 and v2c send only a plaintext community string.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between simulation and real-time mode in Packet Tracer?
flashcards.back: Real-time mode runs the network continuously like real hardware; simulation mode pauses and steps through events so each packet's path and headers can be examined.

flashcards.front: What does Follow TCP Stream do in Wireshark?
flashcards.back: It reassembles all segments of one TCP connection and shows the conversation's payload as readable text.

questions.questionText: An SNMP agent sends an unsolicited Trap message to the network management station. On which port does the manager receive it?
options: TCP 161
UDP 161
UDP 162
TCP 443
questions.explanation: Agents listen for Get/Set requests on UDP 161; traps are sent to the manager on UDP 162.

questions.questionText: Which Wireshark display filter shows only packets whose TCP source or destination port is 80?
options: tcp.port == 80
port 80
ip.port = 80
http.port 80
questions.explanation: tcp.port == 80 is display-filter syntax; port 80 is BPF capture-filter syntax, and the other two are invalid.

questions.questionText: MRTG reads a router interface's ifInOctets counter twice, 60 seconds apart, and the counter has increased by 7,500,000. If the interface speed is 10 Mbps, what is the inbound utilisation?
What is SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) used for?
options: Sending e-mail
Managing and monitoring network devices such as routers, switches and servers
Browsing the web
Transferring files
questions.explanation: SNMP lets a management station read counters and status from agents on network devices, change their settings and receive their alerts (traps). E-mail uses SMTP, the web uses HTTP and file transfer uses FTP or SFTP.

questions.questionText: What does MRTG (Multi Router Traffic Grapher) do?
options: It polls devices for traffic counters and graphs network bandwidth usage over time
It captures and decodes individual network packets
It encrypts file transfers
It manages e-mail delivery
questions.explanation: MRTG reads interface octet counters by SNMP, by default every 5 minutes, and publishes daily, weekly, monthly and yearly traffic graphs as web pages. Capturing and decoding packets is what Wireshark does.

questions.questionText: What kind of traffic analysis can be performed with PRTG Network Monitor (originally Paessler Router Traffic Grapher)?
options: Decrypting the packets of secure web pages
Resolving IP addresses to domain names
Monitoring bandwidth usage and device performance through sensors, with alerts
Verifying that e-mail traffic is encrypted
questions.explanation: PRTG collects bandwidth, availability and health data (via SNMP, WMI, flow data and packet sniffing) into sensors, graphs them and raises alerts. It cannot decrypt HTTPS traffic, and name resolution is DNS's job.

questions.questionText: In SNMP, what is an agent?
options: The central station that polls the devices and draws the graphs
A dedicated cable that carries management traffic
The password (community string) that protects the MIB
Software on a managed device, such as a router or switch, that keeps the device's MIB and answers the manager's requests
questions.explanation: The manager (network management station) sends requests and receives traps, while the agent on each device reads or sets its MIB objects and reports events. The community string is only the shared secret of v1 and v2c.

questions.questionText: What is a MIB in network management?
options: The Management Information Base: the collection of managed objects on a device, each named by an OID, that an SNMP manager can read or set
The maximum interface bandwidth of a router port
A log file of all the packets captured by Wireshark
The encryption key used by SNMPv3
questions.explanation: A MIB defines objects such as sysUpTime, ifInOctets and ifAdminStatus in SMI (ASN.1) and places them in the OID tree. The agent holds their values, and the manager reads or changes them with SNMP.

questions.questionText: Which part of the global OID tree is 1.3.6.1.2.1?
options: private.enterprises, where vendors define their own objects
mib-2, the standard MIB-II objects (iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2)
The interfaces table (ifTable) of MIB-II
The SNMPv3 user-based security (USM) objects
questions.explanation: 1.3.6.1 is iso(1).org(3).dod(6).internet(1), and mgmt(2).mib-2(1) adds .2.1, the root of MIB-II groups such as system (.1) and interfaces (.2). Vendor MIBs live under private.enterprises, 1.3.6.1.4.1.

questions.questionText: The ifInOctets column of the MIB-II interfaces table has the OID 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10. Which OID does MRTG request to read the inbound octet counter of the interface whose ifIndex is 3?
questions.explanation: A table cell is named by the column OID followed by the row index, so ifInOctets for ifIndex 3 is ...1.10.3. The suffix .0 is used only for scalar objects such as sysUpTime.0, and ...2.2.1.3 is a different column (ifType).

questions.questionText: A switch has 24 interfaces (rows 1 to 24 of ifTable). A manager walks the ifInOctets column (i) with GetNext requests only, and (ii) with GetBulk requests using non-repeaters = 0 and max-repetitions = 10. Counting the request that shows the column has ended, how many requests does each walk need?
questions.explanation: GetNext returns one row per request, and the 25th request returns an OID beyond the column, which ends the walk. Each GetBulk returns 10 bindings: rows 1-10, rows 11-20, then rows 21-24 plus 6 bindings past the column, so 3 requests.

questions.questionText: A GetBulkRequest lists three variables, sysUpTime, ifInOctets and ifOutOctets, with non-repeaters = 1 and max-repetitions = 10. Assuming the interface table has more than 10 rows and the reply fits in one message, how many variable bindings does the response contain?
questions.explanation: The first variable (the non-repeater) is returned once, and each of the R = 2 remaining variables is repeated M = 10 times: N + M x R = 1 + 10 x 2 = 21. 30 treats all three as repeaters, and 11 repeats only one of them.

questions.questionText: An administrator's SNMP manager sets ifAdminStatus.5 on a switch to down(2), shutting interface 5. Which SNMP operation does it use?
options: GetRequest
Trap
GetNextRequest
SetRequest
questions.explanation: SetRequest writes a new value to a MIB object, here the interface's administrative status. Get and GetNext only read values, and a Trap is an unsolicited alert from the agent to the manager.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between an SNMP Trap and an InformRequest?
options: A Trap is sent by the manager and an Inform by the agent
An Inform is acknowledged by the receiving manager with a Response and is retransmitted if no reply arrives; a Trap is sent once and never acknowledged
A Trap uses UDP port 161 and an Inform uses TCP port 162
An Inform reads a value from the agent, while a Trap writes one
questions.explanation: Both are notifications sent to the manager, normally to UDP port 162; Inform, introduced in SNMPv2, adds acknowledgement and retries so that events are not silently lost. Reading and writing values are done with Get and Set.

questions.questionText: Why does SNMP use UDP rather than TCP?
options: UDP guarantees that every trap reaches the manager
TCP cannot carry OIDs
Each poll is one small request and reply, the manager handles timeouts and retries itself, and a connectionless protocol keeps working when the network is congested or failing
UDP encrypts the community string
questions.explanation: With no handshake or connection state, a manager can poll thousands of agents cheaply, and management traffic still gets through when links are overloaded. The price is that lost messages must be caught by the manager's own timers, which is why Inform was added for notifications.

questions.questionText: An attacker captures an SNMPv2c SetRequest that a manager sends to a router. What can the attacker most likely do next?
options: Read the read-write community string in plain text from the packet and use it to change the router's settings
Nothing, because SNMPv2c encrypts every message with AES
Only read the router's uptime, because Set messages hide their contents
Nothing, because community strings are hashed before they are sent
questions.explanation: SNMPv1 and v2c send the community string, their only credential, unencrypted in every message, so one captured Set exposes write access. SNMPv3 at the authPriv level prevents this.

questions.questionText: Which SNMPv3 security level provides both authentication of messages and encryption of their contents?
options: noAuthNoPriv
authNoPriv
privNoAuth
authPriv
questions.explanation: SNMPv3's User-based Security Model has three levels: noAuthNoPriv (user name only), authNoPriv (HMAC authentication) and authPriv (authentication plus AES or DES encryption). Privacy without authentication is not defined.

questions.questionText: MRTG polls a 32-bit ifInOctets counter 300 s apart and reads 4,294,000,000 and then 2,000,000. Assuming the counter wrapped exactly once, what is the average inbound rate over the interval?
options: About 53.3 kbit/s
About 79.1 kbit/s
About 9.9 kbit/s
About 114.5 Mbit/s
questions.explanation: Delta = 2^32 - 4,294,000,000 + 2,000,000 = 2,967,296 octets, so the rate = 8 x 2,967,296 / 300 = 79,128 bit/s. Using only the second reading gives 53.3 kbit/s, forgetting the factor 8 gives 9.9 k, and taking |C2 - C1| gives 114.5 Mbit/s.

questions.questionText: A monitoring tool polls a 32-bit octet counter every 60 s. The counter's increase can be measured correctly only if it stays below 2^32 octets between polls. At full load, on which of these interfaces is the 32-bit counter still usable: 100 Mbps, 400 Mbps and 1 Gbps (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s)?
options: 100 Mbps only
All three, because the tool corrects for counter wraps
100 Mbps and 400 Mbps only
None of the three
questions.explanation: Wrap time = 2^32 x 8 / rate: 343.6 s at 100 Mbps, 85.9 s at 400 Mbps and 34.4 s at 1 Gbps, so only the 1 Gbps counter passes 2^32 octets within 60 s and needs the 64-bit ifHCInOctets counter. Using a 300 s interval would leave only 100 Mbps, and forgetting the factor 8 would wrongly rule out all three.

questions.questionText: Users complain that a 100 Mbps link is slow for a few seconds at a time, yet its MRTG graph never shows more than 60 Mbps. What is the most likely explanation?
options: MRTG plots 5-minute averages, so short bursts at the full 100 Mbps are averaged away
MRTG counts only packets, not bytes, so it under-reports traffic
The link cannot be the problem, because a 60 % peak average proves there is always spare capacity
SNMP counters stop counting while the link is congested
questions.explanation: Each point is the octet-counter change over the 5-minute poll interval divided by 300 s, so a 20-second burst at line rate barely moves the average. Shorter polling intervals, or flow and packet tools, reveal such micro-bursts.

questions.questionText: Over a 300 s interval, the counters of a 100 Mbps full-duplex interface rise by 2,250,000,000 (ifInOctets) and 750,000,000 (ifOutOctets). Taking 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s, what are the inbound and outbound utilisations?
options: In 80 %, out 80 %
In 60 %, out 20 %
questions.explanation: Inbound = 8 x 2.25 x 10^9 / 300 = 60 Mbps = 60 % and outbound = 8 x 0.75 x 10^9 / 300 = 20 Mbps = 20 %, since each direction of a full-duplex link has its own 100 Mbps. Adding them (80 %) treats the link as half duplex, 7.5 % forgets the factor 8, and 57.2 % uses 1 Mbps = 2^20 bit/s.

questions.questionText: In PRTG Network Monitor, what is a sensor?
options: A hardware probe that must be plugged into every switch
One monitored measurement on a device, such as the traffic on one switch port, a ping time or a disk's free space
A Wireshark capture filter
The SNMP community string of a device
questions.explanation: PRTG organises monitoring as devices with sensors, each sensor collecting one set of values with its own graphs and alert limits. Licences are counted in sensors, and the free edition allows 100.

questions.questionText: PRTG must monitor CPU load and disk usage on Windows servers on which SNMP is not installed. Which data source does it normally use?
options: WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation)
NetFlow
Packet sniffing on a mirror port
SNMP traps
questions.explanation: WMI exposes Windows performance and configuration data to authorised remote queries, so PRTG's WMI sensors need no SNMP agent. NetFlow and packet sniffing describe network traffic, not a server's CPU or disks.

questions.questionText: In Cisco Packet Tracer, which mode lets a student step through a ping hop by hop and open each PDU to see its OSI-layer details?
options: Realtime mode
Promiscuous mode
Simulation mode
Monitor mode
questions.explanation: Simulation mode pauses the clock and records events in the Event List, so each packet can be advanced and inspected layer by layer. Realtime mode runs like a live network, and promiscuous and monitor modes belong to packet capture on real interfaces.

questions.questionText: A student has no lab equipment but wants to build a three-router network, configure OSPF with IOS commands and check that it works. Which tool fits best?
options: Wireshark
MRTG
PRTG
Cisco Packet Tracer
questions.explanation: Packet Tracer simulates Cisco routers, switches and end devices, including a large subset of IOS commands, so designs can be tested without hardware. Wireshark, MRTG and PRTG observe real networks and cannot build one.

questions.questionText: Which Wireshark capture filter (BPF syntax) records only DNS traffic to or from the host 10.0.0.5?
options: ip.addr == 10.0.0.5 && dns
host 10.0.0.5 and port 53
host == 10.0.0.5 and port == 53
dns.host 10.0.0.5
questions.explanation: Capture filters use BPF primitives such as host, net, port, tcp and udp, combined with and, or and not; port 53 covers DNS over both UDP and TCP. ip.addr == 10.0.0.5 && dns is a valid display filter, but it cannot be used as a capture filter.

questions.questionText: Which Wireshark display filter shows only the first segment of each TCP connection attempt (SYN set, ACK not set)?
options: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0
tcp.flags.syn == 1
tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0
tcp.syn = 1 and ack = 0
questions.explanation: tcp.flags.syn == 1 alone also matches the server's SYN-ACK, so the ACK bit must be tested as well. tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 is capture-filter (BPF) syntax, and the last option is valid in neither.

questions.questionText: An analyst runs Wireshark in promiscuous mode on a PC connected to an ordinary port of a switched Ethernet LAN. Which traffic can she capture?
options: Every frame on the LAN, because promiscuous mode makes the switch copy all traffic to her port
Only frames addressed to her own MAC address, because promiscuous mode has an effect only on hubs
Only frames the switch sends to her port: her own traffic plus broadcasts, multicasts and flooded unknown-unicast frames; to see other hosts' traffic she needs a SPAN (mirror) port or a tap
All traffic on the LAN, but only the headers and never the payloads
questions.explanation: Promiscuous mode only stops her own network card from discarding frames addressed to other MACs; the switch still forwards each known unicast frame only to its destination's port. Port mirroring (SPAN) or a tap delivers copies of other hosts' traffic.

questions.questionText: What does Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream' do?
options: It starts a new capture that records only new TCP connections
It traces the route of a TCP connection hop by hop, like traceroute
It decrypts the TLS records of an HTTPS session without needing any keys
It filters the capture to one TCP connection (tcp.stream eq N) and shows its reassembled payload as a conversation in both directions
questions.explanation: It applies the display filter tcp.stream eq N and shows the bytes of that connection in order, client and server data in different colours, which makes protocols such as HTTP, SMTP or FTP easy to read. Encrypted TLS payloads stay unreadable unless the session keys are supplied.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Wireshark's colouring rules is correct?
options: They are display-filter expressions that paint matching rows in the packet list, for example highlighting TCP retransmissions, and they do not change what is captured or saved
They decide which packets are captured and which are dropped
They encrypt the packets of different protocols with different keys
They can be set only in tcpdump, before the capture starts
questions.explanation: Each rule pairs a display filter with foreground and background colours; the default 'Bad TCP' rule, for instance, marks retransmissions, duplicate ACKs and zero windows. Colouring affects only how the rows are shown.

questions.questionText: Which tcpdump command captures traffic to or from port 443 on interface eth0, without resolving addresses to names, and saves it to a file for later analysis in Wireshark?
options: tcpdump -i eth0 -n -r tls.pcap port 443
tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w tls.pcap port 443
tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w tls.pcap tcp.port == 443
tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 443 -w tls.pcap
questions.explanation: -i chooses the interface, -n turns off name resolution, -w writes raw packets to a pcap file and port 443 is the BPF filter. -r reads an existing file, tcp.port == 443 is display-filter syntax, and -c 443 would stop after 443 packets of any kind.

questions.questionText: What does a NetFlow record, exported by a router to a collector, contain?
options: A full copy of every packet, including its payload
Only the total octet counters of each interface, as SNMP gives
A summary of one flow: its key fields (source and destination IP and port, protocol, ToS, input interface) with packet and byte counts and start and end times
A copy of the router's routing table
questions.explanation: The router groups packets that share the key fields into flows and exports one record per flow over UDP, so a collector can show which hosts and applications use the bandwidth. No payload is exported, which keeps the data small.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Wireshark is NOT correct?
options: It can read passwords sent by unencrypted protocols such as Telnet or HTTP
It decodes protocols layer by layer, from the Ethernet frame up to the application data
It can open capture files saved by tcpdump
It can block or modify packets passing through the interface in real time, like a firewall
questions.explanation: Wireshark is a passive analyser: it copies packets from the capture driver (libpcap or Npcap) and never alters or blocks the live traffic. It does decode hundreds of protocols, show plaintext credentials and read tcpdump's pcap files.
